I do not want to labour this question. I cannot for the life of me, feeling my responsibility, not as a member of the House but as a member of society, get away from the fact that has burned into my soul, that notwithstanding all the laws man can make I still am responsible in a measure and am my brother's keeper. That being true, if

Capital Punishment
means can be evolved by which society will be protected-and that is absolutely the only legitimate reason for punishment, the protection of society-if society can be protected as well by life imprisonment as it can by a second killing, then I say let us adopt the life imprisonment.
But there is another thing. Innocent men have been hanged, and they have been hanged in Canada. Now would it not have been better if the innocent man had been imprisoned for life, and was in a position where the state could make restitution so far as possible for the wrong done to him?
Perhaps there is even higher ground than that. Mankind is universally good. There is something good in every one of God's creatures; there is no question about that; and if, society being protected all the time, an opportunity may be given to the criminal to make himself right not only with his Maker but with the rest of humanity, is it not wise and in the interests of the world that that opportunity should be given?
There is anothe? thought that comes to my mind, and it has been very forcibly expressed by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan). I have said that innocent men have been hanged. There is no doubt in the world also, that guilty men are abroad in the land to-day. Why? For the reason given by my hon. friend from Cumberland, because jurymen dislike very much to take the responsibility of sending to the gallows a man as to whose guilt there may be the least shadow of a doubt, and they have in consequence erred the other way. I would do it myself if I were on a jury. I say that society is not protected nearly as much by maintaining the death penalty as it would be if the death penalty were abolished. I feel that I am not a sentimentalist at all on this question. It is not a question of sentiment; I am viewing it along the broad lines of endeavouring, first, to protect society to the utmost; that is a duty we owe to society; secondly, to prevent the slightest possibilty of an innocent man being convicted and hanged; and thirdly, to give the man himself, if he has been found guilty, a chance to make himself right in the years that are before him.

Mr. Speaker, I have for some years taken some interest in this question. Last year I listened with a good deal of interest to what the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) had to say, and again to-day. I cannot say that I can follow him entirely in all of his opinions; for example, when he regards crime as altogther a manifestation of disease, I 82 i
cannot follow him all the way. At the same time I am in favour of the bill which he presents to-day; I am not in favour of capital punishment.
To my mind there are only three possible reasons that can be advanced for the imposition of capital punishment. The first one, is that of revenge; the second is to prevent a repetition of the crime by the culprit himself; and the third is to deter others from committing murder. That of revenge I think is hardly worthy of consideration in a civilized nation; individuals perhaps may be excused by us for exercising revenge, but surely it is not excusable for a nation or a nation's representatives to take revenge upon one individual.
Then we come to the other reason, to prevent a repetition of the crime by the culprit himself. As has been stated here, repetition can be prevented by other means such as life imprisonment.
Then there is the argument that we should execute the murderer because that will deter others from committing a murder. I am not at all satisfied that that is the case. I have given some attention to statistics; I am not going 'to review them or present them to-day, but I am fairly well convinced that capital punishment does not deter criminals from committing murder. I do not believe in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred that a murderer when he commits the crime is thinking of the death penalty attached to it at all. The greatest preventive of murder is to inculcate in the people themselves a reverence for human life.
If I should summarize the arguments against the infliction of capital punishment, my summary would perhaps be this: One reason has been urged by the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), to give the criminal himself a chance. In a Christian country I suppose that is a perfectly proper sentiment. Personally, although I am not going to place myself outside of the category to which I have just referred, I must admit that consideration for the criminal is about the last thought I have in mind. When I am asking for the abolition of capital punishment I am not thinking of that particularly, but I am willing to give that its fair consideration, because, after all, even the worst of criminals should be given some opportunity of retrieving himself. I am willing to say that. Secondly, there is the possibility of irretrievable error, the possibility that an innocent man may be hanged. Third, there is the disgrace that attaches to the family and relatives of the condemned person, and I think that is worthy of consideration.
Capital Punishment

But the greatest reason of all to my mind, and the one reason why I oppose capital punishment, is that the whole in-5 p m. stitution is an affront to the community itself. It is not necessary for me to speak of the horrors attending an execution; that has already been done to-day by the hon. member for East Calgary. To condemn a man to a strangling shocking death, and submit his body to the indignity which hanging imposes is, I think, repellent and repugnant to every person. We have had in my home city of Kitchener two hangings, the last one some two or three years ago, and I know from personal experience that for perhaps a week or less prior to the execution itself there was in the subconscious or perhaps the conscious mind of every person in that community, man, woman, and child, a growing horror of what was going to take place upon a certain day and at a certain hour. That horror increased from day to day until the gruesome tragedy was completed at the time appointed. That feeling was not merely because a man was to die, but it was because of the manner of his death. We may know, as we frequently do, that a certain person in the community must die by reason of some fatal illness; we take that in a philosophical way; perhaps we have regrets; we sympathize with the person and with his people, but there is not the horror we experience in connection with a hanging. But we Shrink instinctively, I think, from a practice which outrages in one of our kind the dignity and respect that we have for the human body and for human life.
That briefly, Mr. Speaker, is my argument against capital punishment. I would like to say this, in conclusion: If we must have capital punishment, we surely ought to change the method of inflicting it. The practice of hanging, to my mind, is about as barbarous a one as can be conceived. We ought to adopt some more humane or less barbarous method. I would like to make another suggestion: If capital punishment be continued, let us not only adopt some more humane way, but let us not have these executions take place in the locality in which the murderer or victim has lived. We would then at least escape this condition I have spoken of, this feeling of horror in the minds of everybody who lives near the place of execution. I would suggest a central place of punishment, perhaps the penitentiary, to which all criminals of this kind may be taken and quietly done away with, if it is necessary to continue this barbarous practice- I am in favour of the bill.

About thirty years ago I read an essay by the English novelist Thackeray entitled " On going to see a man hanged," and I think from that time until the present I have never had any real doubts as to the barbarity and cruelty of the antiquated system we are still following. I wonder if the House would bear with me if I read a few sentences from that essay which was written in England eighty-four years ago. Listen to this, a bit of the grimmest satire you can find anywhere:
If a public execution is beneficial-and beneficial it is no doubt, or else the wise laws would not encourage 40,000 people to witness it,-the next useful thing must be a full description of such a ceremony, and all its entourages, and to this end the above pages are offered to the reader. How does an individual man feel under it? In what way does he observe it,-how does he view' all the phenomena connected with it,-what induces him, in the first instance, to go and see it,- and how is he moved by it afterwards? The writer has discarded the magazine "we" altogether, and spoken face to face with the reader, recording every one of the impressions felt by him as honestly as he could.
I may say by way of explanation that this is a paragraph towards th^ end of the essay. Continuing he says:
I must confess, then, (for "I" is the shortest word, and the best in this case), that the sight has left on my mind an extraordinary feeling of terror and shame. It seems to me that I have been abetting an act of frightful wickedness and violence performed by a set of men against one of their fellow's; and I pray God that it may soon be out of the power of any man in England to witness such a hideous and degrading sight. Forty thousand (persons (say the Sheriffs), of all ranks and degrees,-mechanics, gentlemen, pickpockets, members of both Houses of parliament, street-walkers, newspapers-writers, gather together before Newgate at a very early hour; the most part of them give up their natural quiet night's rest, in order to partake of this hideous debauchery, which is more exciting than sleep, or than wine, or the last new ballet, or any other amusement they can have. Pickpocket and peer each is tickled by the sight alike, and has that hidden lust after blood which influences our race. Government, a Christian government, gives us a feast every now and then: it agrees-that is to say- a majority in the two Houses agrees-that for certain crimes it is necessary that a man should be hanged by the neck. Government commits the criminal's soul to the mercy of God, stating that here on earth he is to look for no mercy; keeps him for a fortnight to prepare, provides him with a clergyman to settle his religious matters (if there be time enough, but government can't wait); and on a Monday morning, the bell tolling the clergyman reading out the word of God, "I am the resurrection and the life", "The Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away",-on a Monday morning, eight o'clock this man is placed under a beam, with a rope connecting it and him; a plank disappears from under him, and those who have paid for good places may see the hands of the government agent, Jack Ketch, coming up from his black hole, and seizing the prisoner's legs, and pulling them, until he is quite dead-strangled.
I shall also read a few lines at the very end of the essay.
This is the 20th July and I may be permitted for my part to declare that, for the last fourteen days, so

Capital Punishment
salutary has the impression of the butchery been upon me. I have had the man's face continually before my eyes; that I can see Mr. Ketch at this moment, with an easy air, taking the rope from his pocket; that I feel myself ashamed and degraded at the brutal curiosity which took me to that brutal sight; and that I pray to Almighty God to cause this disgraceful sin to pass from among us, and to cleanse our land of blood.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I desire to refer to a copy of an address delivered on the 18th of October, 1922, by George W . Kirchwey, a former warden of the Sing Sing penitentiary in the United States, at an American Prison Association meeting at Detroit, Michigan. He opens by stating that there are three general arguments that have been advanced on behalf of capital punishment. As those have been already dealt with to-day, I shall not further refer to them. Continuing he says:
The argument for the elimination of the murderer as a menace to society is founded on an assumption which everyone who has an intimate knowledge of men convicted of murder knows to be baseless, namely, that murderers are murderers by nature, prone to kill, and that they constitute a professional class like burglars, pickpockets, robbers and the like. Both these types may be represented among those whom the law has branded as murderers, but they constitute an insignificant fraction of the total number. Among the thirty men whom I knew in the death-house at Sing Sing and the 200 or more who were "doing life", I found only a half dozen who seemed to answer that description- one of them a reputed "gunman" from New York city, who became violently insane a few days before his execution, and the other the only person I ever knew who seemed entirely devoid of any sentiment of pity or sympathy and who was diagnosed by the physicians as a psycopathic personality. Doubtless the execution of these two was no loss to the world, but most of the others seemed to me to be of the type described by Sir Basil Thompson, the head of the British Secret Service (Scotland Yard), in his recent work "You have to be in charge of a prison," he says, "in order to realize that the murderer is rarely a criminal by nature at all. But for the grace of God he is just you and I, only more unlucky. Most murders are committed without any deep laid plot... The murderer is repentant, and is planning only how he can earn an honest living after he is discharged."
If this seems a bit too sweeping, let me assure you that it is far nearer the truth than is the popular conception of the murderer. I made it my business to know every man in the death-house while I was at Sing Sing. The only characteristic that they had in common was that they were sick, tortured souls over whom hung the pall of the awful fate that awaited them. Only a few of them were criminals in the ordinary sense of the term and one, whose death sentence had been commuted to imprisonment for life, complained to me of the fact that he was in a situation where he could get so little decent companionship, there w'ere so many crooks. A few of my murderers were obviously feeble-minded, a few apparently insane or psychopathic, but most were of the kind described by Sir Basil Thompson,-men who, but for the accident of fate-some jam in the wheels of life, some uprush of upsetting emotion, some bewilderment of faculties- might have been even as you and I are this day.
Further on he quotes from Governor Davis as follows:	; x, |[ ji
It is thus easily to be seen that, on the whole, it appears to make little difference in the prevalence or scarcity of homicides whether the punishment is death or life imprisonment. In fact, there would seem to be a slight lessening of homicides where no death penalty exists. At any rate, these figures tend definitely to show that the deterrent of capital punishment is largely mythical and merely an imaginary factor.
Then he proceeds to discuss the question from the point of view expressed in the statement : " Eliminate murder, not the murderer," but I shall quote no further.
I noticed, not many weeks ago, in the Ottawa Citizen, the following letter, which I think, was taken from one of the American papers. It appeared to me to be so pertinent to the question under discussion to-day, which I then thought might come up at some future date, that I clipped it out, and I should like to read to the House one or two paragraphs from it. The letter is entitled "What is prison for?":
I take it that most of us no longer believe in the theory of punishment. We put people in jail because we believe they are dangerous to the community. Accordingly, we should let them out as soon as we have reason to believe that they are no longer dangerous. It may be quite evident that the man who has killed is never going to do it again and that the shoplifter will continue in his usual pursuit as soon as he is released. In that case it seems to me quite silly to keep the murderer in the jail for life and to let the shoplifter go.
If we had judges and wardens wise enough, there might be just one universal sentence for all criminals. Each would be sentenced to remain in prison until cured.
The subject has been so completely covered to-day that I do not think it is necessary for me to speak any further. I trust that the government will leave this matter to be settled by the House after a full and free discussion, and that this House may take the humane and Christian view which, I think, has been so well expressed to-day by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham). I listened with singular pleasure and satisfaction to his concise and complete statement of the case in favour of the abolition of capital punishment.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to speak on this matter, but as the argument is getting into the sentimental line, much can be said for and against capital punishment. Before I would vote in favour of this bill, I would ask that there be more amendments to our criminal code, guaranteeing that every murderer, every man who is premeditating murder, such as those who are now rampant in the country, engaged in robbing banking institutions particularly, to enrich themselves so that they can live in luxury for the balance
Capital Punishment

of their lives, can be kept in chains or caged and compelled to work twelve or fifteen hours a day, so that he may earn enough to cover the expense that it would take to keep him from ever again becoming a prey upon society. It might be possible to make society perfectly secure in this regard by using chains, shackles or cages, but until that safeguard has been effected, I shall have to vote against the bill.

Would the hon.
gentleman apply that same rule to those who rob banks from the inside as well as to those who rob them from the outside?

Certainly. If you find
murderers on the inside as well as the outside, I would apply the same rule. I would have them work for the state for at least twelve or fifteen hours in every twenty-four, and have shackles on their feet while they were not working, and possibly even while they were working. But I would have them so that they could never escape and prey upon innocent society again in their lives.

Mr. Speaker, if my memory serves me well, I have had an opportunity, on at least three occasions, of listening to a debate on this question during the last twenty-five years or so, and of voting once or twice on this question. I, therefore, consider it my duty to give a word of explanation. In a matter like this, I would be guided, not by sentiment, but by eminent men, legal men who have given up their lives to the study of law, and that is the reason why I asked the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) to give me the authority of any attorney general of any province of Canada or any attorney general of Canada who had ever advocated the abolition of the death penalty. We are not turning our eyes to the United States now for precedents in these matters. Great Britain is good enough for us yet, and I hope she will continue to be for a long time. Great Britain has not abolished the death penalty, for good reasons, no doubt.
The constituency which I have the.honour to represent 'and have represented for a quarter of a century, has not seen an execution in fifty years. When I was a young boy, employed in Montreal in newspaper work, I acted for some years as coroner's clerk. One morning, in fulfilment of my duties, I had to go down to witness the first execution that had taken place in Montreal in twenty years. It was an extraordinary thing to see an

execution in those days. This man had committed his crime while serving a term in the penitentiary, and while he was comparatively a young man, twenty-five or twenty-six years of age, he had spent some fifteen years of his life in jail or penitentiary. Conditions are no better now than they were then. We must admit that since the Great War, things are not much better than they used to be. There is a looseness of morals the world over, a condition of things which is really discouraging.. What happened in Montreal last week is something that is worth while pondering over? At two o"cloek, in broad daylight on Ontario street, one of the most frequented thoroughfares of the city, three or four young men, engaged in the fulfilment of their duties, were held up by half a dozen gunmen and shot at, one, the sole support of his mother, shot like a dog. The other man, Stone, who was shot at the same time, had a penitentiary record of twelve different institutions. He was then unfortunately under bail for a crime which he had committed.
As regards the idea of changing this punishment to life imprisonment, life imprisonment does not always mean what its words contain. The Crown always has the right to revise the sentence passed upon a man serving a sentence of life imprisonment, and I have in mind the case of Morin, of Montmagny, whose name will be familiar to the Minister of Justice. This man was granted a reprieve on the eve of his execution, and he was sentenced to St. Vincent de Paul penitentiary, where, after ten years, on the recommendation of the late Sir John Thompson, he was liberated. Life imprisonment, therefore, may mean a very short term. No man wishes to have capital punishment carried out if that can be avoided. The jury that are called on to try a man charged with murder are told, in effect, in the last words that fall from the judge's mouth:	"If you have a reasonable
doubt, it is your sworn duty to give the benefit of that doubt to the accused." When the verdict is given by the jury and the judge is called upon to pronounce the sentence, he has to write out a full report of his notes and to transmit the evidence to the Department of Justice, where that is scanned carefully by men who are experts in such matters. The minister himself has to examine into the case and the Privy Council has to do likewise. The great majority of capital sentences, or, I should suppose, at least half of them, are never carried out, but they are cases, not for the sake of revenge, because the state is not looking for revenge, but for the sake of preventing repetition, as a deterrent and for the protection of society-

Capital Punishment
Is the hon. gentleman prepared to say that the statement of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham)) is wrong, that men who are innocent have been hanged in Canada?

No doubt
men have been hanged for what we to-day do not regard as offences. I could mention some who were hanged for political crimes and whom nowadays we consider heroes, monuments being erected in memory of them in the public squares of large cities. It depends upon the point of view. But we are proceeding on the old theory that it is better that ninety-nine guilty persons should escape than that one innocent man should be convicted. As the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) said a moment ago, the great Judge is the judge of all; but I do not think that the Department of Justice in Canada is willing to admit-at least I have not heard that the admission has been made-that any really innocent person has been convicted, or, as it is said in French, that an erreure judiciare has been committed.
I do not recollect anything of that kind. But in view of what is happening now in the Mother Country and in Canada, and in view of the complete absence of any recommendation, for a change in the mode of punishment, from any legal authority in this country, from any judicial mind, or from those who are trained to deal with such cases, I think the time is ill-chosen to bring about a change in this respect. I certainly will vote to sustain the institution as it is.

I want to make a few brief remarks on the subject matter of this bill, though I quite realize that the question has been covered most amply in the very eloquent and learned discourse with which the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) has favoured the House, and also in the very able remarks which have been addressed to us by the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) and the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). There are however a few observations which at this time it may be fitting to make, especially in reply to the hon. gentleman who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Marcil, Bonaventure). The hon. gentleman said that in regard to this matter he would take the views of legal men. Now, I have a high respect for legal men; I feel that there are few classes in the community who deserve so well of their fellow-citizens. But I am sorry to say that in the past legal men, especially when they have mounted the bench, have not been the best authorities for
one to accept as regards the advisability of change or reform. Lord Ellenborough was one who spoke against the abolition of the death penalty for petty theft, as was well explained this afternoon by the member for East Calgary. And I regret to say that in a discussion of this question years ago in the Mother Country John Bright was forced to point out that the elimination of the death penalty on many occasions had been brought about in the Old Country in the face of the opposition, if not of all at least of a great number of the judges, who were anxious that it should be retained for the punishment of crimes which are now considered trifling.
I was somewhat interested in hearing the hon. member (Mr. Marcil, Bonaventure) declare that institutions that existed in Great Britain were institutions which we should unhesitatingly and unquestioningly accept. My mind instantly turned to the hereditary House of Lords in England, and I wondered whether the hon .member would be willing to see such an institution created and perpetuated in this country. My hon. friend's views in regard to the institutions of Great Britain are hot very consistent. When the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) adduced, as an argument in favour of the divorce bill which he had before the House the other day, the fact that his bill was on all fours with legislation that presently existed in Great Britain, the hon. member for Boniaventure opposed it.

I might be permitted to
point out for the benefit of the member for Bonaventure that there is at present before the British House of Commons an application similar to the one under discussion in this House for the abolition of capital punishment.

That being the case,
if such legislation is passed in Great Britain the hon. member for Bonaventure would consistently support a similar measure in this House. The hon. gentleman is not altogether consistent in his admiration for things Britannic. He said that he would sustain the present institution, in view of the things that were happening in the Motherland. I wonder, does he refer to the coming into power in Great Britain of the Labour government? Does that fill his mind with dread? I trust not; because I think the people in all the nations of the British Commonwealth view that circumstance with a good deal of satisfaction and hope for the future of the British race, and wish that government well. As long as seventy years ago one of the best, the wisest and the most characteristically English
Capital Punishment

of British statesmen, the late Right Hon. John Bright, strongly supported the abolition of the death penalty.
The arguments in favour of the principle are, I think, overwhelming. Surely, all civilized people admit that the only sound argument in support of the retention of the extreme penalty is that it is a deterrent; and surely the burden of proof is upon those who urge its retention. My examination of the question leads me to the belief that capital punishment is not a deterrent. Who would be the best judges as to whether the death penalty was or was not a deterrent? Would it not be those men of education and character whose position at the head of penitentiaries would bring them into contact with murderers? The opinion of a judge sitting on the bench that the death penalty is desirable has not the same weight as the opinion of a man who by reason of his duty comes into close contact with homicidal criminals. And I think it is pretty well the view of a very large number of men who have served as wardens in penitentiaries that capital punishment does not deter men from murder. In fact, I remember some years ago hearing a very celebrated American warden of Sing Sing penitentiary-I think his name was Osborne-declare that, far from the death penalty being a deterrent, it had entirely the opposite effect; for whenever a man went to the electric chair to expiate the crime of murder he became a hero to the underworld. And the same thought has been brought out this afternoon by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan), who has pointed out that once a man has been condemned to death he is regarded as a martyr rather than a criminal. If, then, capital punishment is not a deterrent there is no other reason for our maintaining this method of punishing human beings. I would respectfully point out to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) that as a matter of fact the imposition of the death penalty is out of date and is not working well at the present time. It is ineffective for reasons which have been placed before the House and which I beg the House's pardon for insisting upon again. To-day in all parts of the country where "twelve good men and true'' are called upon to "a true presentment make between the prisoner at the bar and our sovereign lord, the king," they have such disinclination to the death penalty that they will seize hold of any shred of evidence, or the want of evidence, in order to be able conscientiously to bring in a verdict of not guilty. As the feelings of our people become more and more attuned to higher civilization, it 
will be more and more difficult to find juries who will bring in a verdict of guilty in capital charges.
And not only has it that effect, but in my experience it has influenced those who would otherwise be ready to become judges. I remember in Montreal, during my brief experience as a practising lawyer, it was expected that one of the ablest men of the Montreal bar would be elevated to the Court of Appeal,, and it was common rumour among the lawyers that this gentleman, who would have made a most distinguished judge, refused to accept the position because he would have to deal with criminal cases. He could have given distinguished service to his country, but he did not feel that he could sentence a fellowbeing to capital punishment.
If there is fair ground for believing that the deterrent nature of the death penalty is not satisfactorily proved, then it would appear to me to be well for Canada to put herself in line with other civilized countries and abolish the death penalty. It is not a deterrent because, as I said a moment ago, more and more will juries fail to convict on capital charges. I do not go all the way with my hon. friend from East Calgary in thinking that punishment has no place as a deterrent against crime. I think it has. But I think he is largely right in his view that criminality is very often more of a disease than an expression of premeditated wrong-doing. I think punishment has its place, but it is not the severity of punishment, it is its certainty which is the real deterrent. And if you make punishment so severe that society draws back and refuses to impose it, so far as its deterrent effect is concerned it would be far better to have punishment which is less severe but more certain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week a delegation interviewed the Home Secretary of Great Britain, the Right Hon. Arthur Henderson, a prominent member of the government of which my hon. friend (Mr. Irvine) has spoken so eloquently. Mr. Henderson is a reformer, he is a progressive in every way. This will be generally admitted. But here is the report of the interview which I find in the Morning Post of the 25th March last:
The following official report was issued from the Home Office:
The Home Secretary received this morning a deputation of members of a number of societies who placed before him various considerations and statistics in support of the abolition of the death penalty in this country. The societies in question were: The Committee for the Abolition of the Death Penalty,

Capital Punishment
the Society of Friends, the Women's Co-operative Guild, the Howard League for Penal Reform, the Central Council of Societies Working for the Abolition of Capital Punishment, Manchester Society for Abolition of Capital Punishment, Women's Freedom League, and the British Section of the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom.
Mr. George Lansbury, who introduced the deputation, drew special attention to its representative character as indicating a recent rapid growth of public opinion on the subject.
He was followed by Major Christopher Lowther and Miss Margery Fry, who argued the case in greater detail, and produced various figures.
The Home Secretary, in replying, thanked the deputation for waiting upon him, and for their full statement of their case, and promised that w'hat they had said would be brought before the government in an appropriate form before any decision was reached by the government on the question of abolition. He pointed out, however, that any government must take public opinion into account, and that so far as his long parliamentary experience went there was little evidence of any general public desire for abolition, the subject not having been debated for many years. He also pointed out that before a government could recommend an alteration in that law they would have to consider very carefully what satisfactory alternative punishment they could properly suggest.
As I have stated, Mr. Henderson is the Home Secretary in the British government, and as such he is entrusted with the responsibility of the administration of justice in Great Britain;-perhaps he may have had other views in the past, as I read in a newspaper that the delegates were surprised at his answer, but he has that responsibility. I am in the same position in this country, and I must share the views of Mr. Henderson. As far as my own personal feelings are concerned, by temperament and by instinct I would be inclined to vote for the bill, but from a high sense of duty I feel that I cannot do so, and that for the present we must retain capital punishment. If I were convinced that any other form of punishment would be as effective for the protection of the Canadian people, it would be my duty to recommend its adoption. It is because I do not believe that capital punishment can be replaced by any other form of punishment which would be as effective that I am forced to take this stand.
I have listened with a great deal of interest to the remarks of my hon. friend from East Calgary. He is to be congratulated on the manner in which he has expressed his views. This question has engaged the attention of the students of sociology in all the civilized countries in the world, and there have always been great differences of opinion with regard to it. Arguments of great weight can be adduced on both sides. Statistics can be produced, but statistics in this matter are unsatisfactory and inconclusive. Apart from
the form of punishment we must consider the race, the customs of the people, the climate, the environment generally-all these considerations must be had in mind when you deal with statistics produced in favour of or against capital punishment. The countries which are most similar to ours so far as the mentality or the make-up of the people is concerned are Great Britain and the United States. I happened to lay my hand on a very able article in The English Review of September last, written by Major J. B. Paget on the "Death Penalty in Time of War," in which the w'riter quotes some statistics. Major Paget says that during the war the death penalty was necessary in the army to prevent desertion. He said that the percentage of Australian deserters was about four times that of the English. I quote from the article:
I tried to find out the reason, and came to the conclusion that it was owing to Australia having no death penalty for desertion. In the New Zealand forces, on the other hand, they having the death penalty, the percentage of deserters was even smaller than the English.
He points out that in the beginning there was no death penalty for desertion from the Canadian army and that a rather large number of desertions took place; then they brought in the death penalty and the percentage sank to the same as the English. He found the same situation in the American army. He says that the greatest deterrent against desertion in the army is the death penalty. He points out also that so far as the civil population is concerned, in time of peace the United1 States, with the population of 110,000,000, has some 8,000 murders a year. Of those convicted for murder, Major Paget says,-and this has been stated also by my hon. friend who proposes this bill-only a certain proportion are executed. He goes on to say:
In the British Isles the death penalty has hitherto been inflicted on the great majority of convicted murderers. With a population of some 46,000,000, not more than about 200 murders are committed annually.
And he adds:
The unwritten law and brainstorms cut little ice with a British jury.
Eight thousand murders in the United States with a population of 110,000,000; two hundred murders in the British Isles with a population of 46,000,000. Here in Canada where we have the death penalty and where it is enforced we have had for the last ten years an average of twenty-five murders per year, which is less than three per million of the population. These figures are a decisive answer, it seems to me, to many of the argu-
Capital Punishment

ments advanced this afternoon. These are from countries which are similar to ours, and I do not think they can be successfully challenged.
I would not wish anybody to think that capital punishment is carried out in the spirit of retaliation, or revenge, or vengeance- It is not for that purpose, and that is not the consideration which influences me in favouring a continuance of capital punishment. It is as a deterrent; and whatever may bo said I am convinced that it is a deterrent. After all, every human being values life more highly than anything else, and even the dumb animals recoil from death. It is a deterrent, and it is a protection of society. If only one innocent human life is saved through capital punishment, I think it is our duty to maintain it on the statutes of this country.
Canada has an immense territory which is sparsely populated and there are places where women and children live miles away from the nearest neighbour. These women and children must be protected. We have immigration which brings to this country people from many parts of the world, and statistics in the Department of Justice show that 49 per cent of the murders committed in Canada in recent years have been committed by foreigners. I think capital punishment is a protection and that we should keep it. I repeat that if I could convince myself that imprisonment for life would be just as good, just as effective a punishment as the death penalty, I would be in favour of changing the law in that regard. But I am not convinced of that.
Would the minister be good enough to give the House one proof that capital punishment is a deterrent? That is the ground upon which he says he favours it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I have given statistics
and I have stated my firm conviction. My hon. friend has given his opinion and I am giving mine- If I were moved only by sentimental and humanitarian feelings I would vote with my hon. friend, but my best judgment and my conscience tell me that I cannot support the proposal embodied in his bill.

Can the
minister tell the House that in any case where the death penalty was imposed the victim asked that it be changed to life imprisonment?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
They all ask for a change of sentence to imprisonment for life.
At six o'clock the House took recess.

(Lunenburg):
Mr. Speaker, before the disposition of this bill takes place on its second reading, I should like to make a very few remarks. Speaking for myself personally, I do not think it is necessary to make any lengthy remarks upon the bill at this stage. This is a very serious matter and-

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member agreed with me that there would be no discussion at this stage of the bill, on condition that I did not speak. The hon. member came across here and agreed with me that there would be no discussion on the second reading.

The only thing I want to do now, and I thought I had made that clear to the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) is to enter this formal protest before the bill receives its second- reading. I do not think anybody can object to that.
That is all right.

I think that is only fair and
proper. I may say that I also am the victim of a misunderstanding with my hon. friend in one particular, because when I went over to see him the day before yesterday and asked him when he intended to introduce this bill he told me, if my memory serves me aright, that it was not going to be introduced until after Easter. So far as I personally am concerned I am quite willing for one or more persons to come before parliament and ask for the incorporation of the United Church of Canada or any other church, but what we do want to do is to protest against the principle of this

speakeroldname: Mr. MURRAY MacLAREN (St. John City and Counties of St. John and Albert):
speechtext:
I have not entered into an arrangement of any kind with the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke), and therefore I feel . perfectly free to speak on the second reading of the bill, but perhaps it may be soothing to my hon. friend to tell him that I do not propose to do so. I do wish, however, to make a few general observations, not by way of discussion.
There is a great deal to be said on this bill, but I consider it more suitable to have the discussion at a later stage, and this is the reason l do not propose to discuss it just now, because as this is a private bill the second reading does not concede the principle of the bill.
One point I wish to mention is this: I do not think that there is objection to the incorporation of the United Church, provided that the church is for those who wish to go into it, and provided further that those who do not so desire may remain in their mother churches.
The other point I wish to mention, because it is a general principle, is this:	There is
objection made, as we know, by Presbyterians that the petitioner for the bill, the Moderator of the General Assembly, has not been authorized by the General Assembly, and even were he so apparently authorized, the General Assembly has no authority to so authorize him. I say this because I wish to draw the attention of the House at once to the fact that this matter is now pending in the Supreme Court of Ontario, and judicial decisions are being sought on the question of the constitutionality of the procedure. The other matter, Mr. Speaker, is that there are many grave complaints made by Presbyterians regarding various other sections of the bill; so much so that I join with the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) in urging that the motion for the second reading of this bill be passed at once, so that the committee may have an opportunity of hearing a full statement of the complaints as they are made by Presbyterians.
Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to the select standing committee on Miscellaneous Private Bills.
The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Irvine for the second reading of Bill No. 3, to amend the Criminal Code.

The value of this debate I think has been already assured. It has elicited from two ministers of the Crown very significant and very impressive speeches. Although they came to different conclusions, it was possible to recognize behind their expressions of opinion a common feeling, I might say a delicacy of feeling, a refinement of sentiment, which it does one good to see in men occupying the positions which they occupy. After listening to those speeches I felt as others must have felt, that the doom of capital punishment has been already pronounced. The speech of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) was as cogent in that direction as the remarks of the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham). He expressed a refinement of sentiment which some of us believe his whole nature is compact with, and I believe that sooner or later that sentiment, which is by no means monopolized by the minister and his colleagues, will see the finish of capital punishment, and of every other summary means of dealing with problems that are really social and not individual in character. I agree with them that sentiment is largely out of place in a discussion of this kind. Nothing can be settled by sentiment, because sentiment beclouds every issue into which it enters, and there is no necessity for bringing sentiment into this argument either on one side or the other. We may appeal to the sentiment of the public, but unfortunately feeling is balanced by fear, and fear is one of those emotions that is just as easily appealed to as sentiment, and if ever you introduce an argument along sentimental lines, another argument is sure to be introduced appealing to fear which overwhelms us immediately, and we do not get anywhere.
I should like to make a few remarks without going over the ground which has already been covered and I desire to base my approach to this question not upon humanitarian grounds, but rather upon, if I may use the word, societarian grounds. I agree with the Minister of Justice that society needs protection, and that it is our duty to protect society, but I disagree with the argument that is implied in his statement.
Capital Punishment

What he means by protecting society is protecting certain individuals in society. Strictly speaking it is not society he is thinking of. He is speaking of certain individuals in society and not of society as a whole. He is speaking of protection in exactly the same sense as the party to my right speaks of protection. It is not protection of society at all. Society is not concerned. It is the individual that is concerned. For many, many generations we have been concentrating all our attention in a blind way trying to protect the individual and we jeopardize society. That is what we have been doing and are doing yet. We are trying to save individual souls, and in the process of doing that we have been consigning multitudes to perdition. That is the way we manage to do things in this topsy-turvy world. My hon. friend from Brome (Mr. McMaster) did well to introduce the name of John Bright into this argument. After all the sentiment behind this appeal is liberalism. In order to perpetuate liberalism and to save liberalism, we have to be liberal all round. John Bright was not liberal in parts; he was liberal in every fibre of his being. When he thought about protecting society he was not thinking of certain individuals in it to the exclusion of others. He was thinking of society as a unit in which he himself existed, and of which he was a part, and with which he felt sympathetic.
I think the time has come for all intelligent communities to begin dealing with causes and not with effects. Crime, however you look at it, is a symptom. Crime, wherever it exists, is a token that something is wrong with society, because the criminal arises from society. He does not make himself, and in order to deal with crime you have to get behind the individual and deal with society for its responsibility. There is, Mr. Speaker, a famous saying of a philosopher who belongs to the same race as the Minister of Justice, that if we knew all we would forgive all. When you see the criminal standing at the bar, he is not nearly so guilty as superficially you think he is, and the public against whom he is supposed to have sinned are not so guiltless as you think they are. No, if we knew all, we perhaps, might not forgive all, but we would forgive a great deal. Forgiveness is not a maudlin sentiment. Forgiveness is recognition by men and women that humanity is one. It is a recognition of the solidarity of society. It is a sympathetic understanding of the mesh-work of relationship in which we all exist, and when one sins, 
all sin, all have sinned. The Great Author of mercy on one occasion gave a dramatic illustration of this. He was present when capital punishment was about to be administered and He said to the judge and jury who were also to be the executioners: "He that is without sin, let him cast the first stone." He did not mean that they were sinners in the sense that the criminal was a sinner, but he meant that they as representing society were responsible. I think we have arrived at that stage in the development of humanity when the most benighted of us have some sense of what it means to have a sympathy as wide as humanity itself, which does not exclude even the criminal, but which looks upon the criminal as our own flesh and blood.
As regards the argument of sentiment, I dislike sentiment, as I said before, when we are dealing with rational matters; but what is sentiment and what is not sentiment? When the time comes for the criminal to approach his death, it is almost invariably the case that the public or a large section of it becomes sentimental, and that sentiment is expressed in many ways. It is the habit to speak lightly of that sentiment, but I do not speak lightly of it. It is not a light thing. What are the facts? On the eve of execution there in that lurid light stands a man, or a woman it may be, of our own flesh and blood belonging to our own race, and in the background you have those terrible realities which the society that has made him what he is has painted to our imagination, rightly or wrongly. I think we all recognize the fact to-day, that is, if we think at all, that this sentiment, which we sometimes deride, is profounder than superficially we may consider it to be. There is the condemned man standing against that background which the teachings of society have impressed upon our imagination and mind, whether it be Catholic or Protestant, whether it be Dante or John Milton. There is that man about to be launched into that terrible condition of things which is at the base of all our convictions. Is that not a time for sentiment? I will guarantee that it is not only the sentimental people who send flowers and notes of condolence to the condemned that feel that sentiment, but other people, more reserved, feel that sentiment as well, who do not express it. I think it is a mark of high development in a man's condition when he feels that sentiment. What kind of a person could be unmoved when, by the volition of society a human soul is cast into conditions like that, which society has, through the ages and generations, instilled into our very convictions and sentiments?

Capital Punishment
Then there is the sentiment in regard to degradation. We all revolt at the thought of delegating one of our fellow citizens to kill another, and rightly so, although I do not agree that under all conditions hanging is degrading. I know plenty of people whom I would like to hang myself. I would like to be on the end of the rope-I mean the other end.
Is that sentiment?

I think my self respect would be in no wise injured by the deed. It is no use arguing that under all circumstances the violence of society is degrading- I am not one of those who believes that stern measures introduced by society, in the interest, not of individuals, but of society for its own protection, not for the protection of any part of it, are wrong. I believe sometimes they are right. I do not think hanging in the days of Walpole, Pitt and Newcastle degraded them in the sense that it degrades us to-day. At any rate, it ought not to be so. If it degraded them then, if they hanged men for stealing sheep or a 25 cent piece or its equivalent, I can see quite clearly that its reaction upon them would probably be trivial as regards its moral significance; but for us in the twentieth century, this is a different matter. People in those times, when hanging became part of the British constitution, believed in political corruption. I cannot conceive of our believing in political corruption in the twentieth century. We are growing out of those things. All history is a proof of that.
There is the argument as to the deterrent value of hanging, and I want to part company here again in a sense from some of the advocates of this bill, because I believe that punishment, even hanging, is a deterrent. All history is very clear proof of that. Unfortunately, sometimes it has deterred the wrong things. Sometimes it deters right things as well as evil things. Sometimes it deters other kinds of criminals than the homicidal criminal. Sometimes it has deterred people who would obtrude themselves into places where they had no right and claim for themselves powers which they had no right to claim. Hanging has had very salutary influences throughout all history; but as I said before, we are getting on. When hanging became part of the British constitution, as some people seemed to think it did, the medical science of that time believed that phlebotomy was the deterrent for influenza and headache- They believed in bloodletting for trivial ailments of all kinds, we have outlived that age. There was a sense in which it was true that bloodletting
cured those ailments; it was a deterrent; but a great deal of water has run under the bridge since those times ,and we have been enlightened in many respects. Surely the time has come when we, civilized people as we are, should be able to adopt better expedients than those. As an expedient I say it has had its day. It has ceased to be effective, and it is a wrong expedient for the age in which we live.
More than that, it is a stultifying expedient. I believe that a condition of society that pins its faith upon curing the criminal by killing him will always have criminals to kill. It is the point of view that is wrong, and so long as you have that crass, unenlightened individualism that blinds you to your social obligations and makes you feel that you stand apart from your fellow men, you will always have a society in which there are criminals. That is the soil out of which criminals spring, the lack of social obligation and the lack of social sympathy, these are the things that create criminals. Unless therefore you get rid of these conditions you will never get anywhere at all. I think it would be well if this country or any other civilized nation would make an experiment in abolishing this outworn expedient, not with the hope that things will be immediately improved.
Unfortunately I cannot entirely share the view of those who are arguing in support of the bill, that the abolition of capital punishment will not involve greater responsibilities on the state than heretofore. The moment capital punishment was abolished" there would devolve a tremendous responsibility upon society, and society would be exposed to a new situation. I will go thus far with the opponents of the bill. But what does that signify to a civilized and enlightened community? It would simply steel people up and put them upon their mettle. I argue for the bill therefore because I think it will help the Canadian people to recognize their social responsibilities and would induce us to remove those conditions that create the criminal. I do not believe in tampering with the constitution or in doing away with institutions if there is nothing of a constructive character to substitute in place of what is rejected. The fault of this individualistic age is that the virtuous men go forth shouting, " down with this and down with the other," and are too individualistic to see that when they have cast out one devil seven others are likely to take its place. I believe that in Canada at the present time there is a sufficiently strong social sentiment and sense of oneness, a sufficiently
Capital Punishment

developed sense of economic justice, for us to be able to dispense with this outworn expedient which is a disgrace to any highly civilized people, and to usher in instead a regime of social improvement and of educative effort that will in time largely eradicate criminal conditions and render criminals just as impossible as the present antiquated method of dealng with them is out of date.
Miss AGNES C. MACPHAIL (Southeast Grey):	Just twice in my life have I come
closely in contact with capital punishment. The first time was the day that I wrote my entrance to normal examination. I will never forget that day; it was in Stratford, Ontario, and as we passed the jail on the way to the collegiate institute the black flag was at half mast and I knew of course that this meant that capital punishment had been executed, that the extreme penalty of the law had been enforced that morning. I have not forgotten the feeling I had then. I felt that society as a whole had deliberately contemplated and taken the life of this man, who it is true had taken the life of another. The second time I came closely in contact with capital punishment was last week and I am not likely to have forgotten the fact so quickly. I was reading about a week ago that they used to hang people in England at one time for picking pockets. They had public executions and the picking of pockets at these public executions became so prevalent that they had to abandon the public execution of pickpockets. When we are trying to teach children to be truthful do we lie to them? I think not. Or if we want to teach people to be honest, do we steal? If we want to teach the hater to love do we hate him? Well, then, if we want to teach people to respect and revere human life, that which we can take away but cannot give, can we do so by taking human life? It seems to me that if we are going to really reverence human life we must as a society refuse to take i't; we must come to the view that punishment should be of a reforming character rather than revengeful. It is true that the taking of life is wrong, but two wrongs do not make a right. To me life is sacred, and because it is such a sacred thing that I personally could not take the life of any one, even though that one had taken the life of another, I support whole heartedly the bill that is before the House.

I am not at all a sanguinary individual; I never had any desire to see the rope around any one's neck. But I do not think there TMr. Bird.)
ever was a more inappropriate time than the present for parliament to take up such a question as that which is under consideration to-day. There are men going around this country shooting anybody who gets in their way, sometimes merely for the purpose of taking money from some individual; and for fear that that individual will defeat their attempt to rob some one else they shoot him, as has happened within the last few days.
And we have capital punishment.
Yes.

Why did it not stop it?
Mr^HOCKEN:	You will not stop it by
making the penalty less than it is to-day, and any one who argues thus is, in my judgment, talking in a perfectly futile way.

Will the hon. member prove
his Statement?

I am going to let it go
with my assertion. There is nothing a man values so much as his own life, whether he be a murderer or not. There is nothing that will deter a man from murdering another so much as the fear of losing his own life. That is the one thing above all others that he desires to protect and preserve, and I cannot agree with those who argue that by removing the penalty of capital punishment we are going to reduce the frequency of murder. Those who argue that capital punishment has not curtailed murder might as well argue that in providing a very excellent home for drunkards and thieves, a place that is very much more a home than a prison, you are creating the very best conditions that can make for the discontinuance of thieving. There is a gaol farm near Thornhill in the province of Ontario where drunkards, thieves and other petty criminals are given every advantage that accrues from living under wholesome conditions and engaging in farm work. They are as well fed as if they were living at the Queen's Hotel; I do not mean to say that the bill of fare is as varied, but it is as wholesome. These men are not overworked, but they are given sufficient exercise to keep them in sound health. But we still have drunkeness and other vices in the province. I would have hon. members understand that I am in favour of dealing with petty criminals in a tender way if there is any hope of reforming them; I would not treat them with unnecessary harshness. But I want to see those who break the laws restrained; they must be restrained. However, those who commit what might be called

Capital Punishment
petty offences, as compared with murder, are well treated all over this country. But that does not stop their criminal career. Men go out of the gaol fawn I am referring to and commit the same offences for which they were first put under restraint. Now, if the application of the golden rule which my hon. friend speaks of were effective, these men should not commit similar offences within a week or two of regaining their freedom.
Has the hon. gentleman studied any statistics showing the proportion of those who after being given their parole do not offend again?

Yes, I believe a great many of these petty criminals do not come back, and on the whole I think the system works out fairly well. I do not mean to say that every criminal on leaving the jail farm resorts immediately to a life of crime. I do not think my hon. friend will argue that every man sent to jail for close confinement goes back to a career of crime immediately on regaining his freedom. Many men have been reformed during the course of their imprisonment. But I am arguing that if, as is claimed by some speakers, gentle treatment is going to reform criminals, such treatment has not so far proved to be a specific in restraining such men from further crime. They have criminal instincts and appear to be incorrigible.
Does the hon. member contend that there is a smaller proportion of real reforms effected under the present so-called lenient system than under the previous system?

No, I do not so contend. I do not know, but I hope that a larger number are reformed under the present system. That is the reason why municipalities in my province spend hundreds of thousands of dollars annually to support such institutions. Every effort is being made to reform the criminally inclined, but crime is still committed. It is all very well to talk about the sacredness of the life of a murderer, but I think we should have some regard for the sacredness of the life of his victim. The man who has no more regard for society and for the sacredness of the life of anyone who stands between him and the possession of a few dollars is, in my opinion, getting no more than just punishment when he is called upon to give up his own life for having committed a cold-blooded murder. Those who argue there is anything cruel about such a sentence I think fail to see the real measure of justice that is behind it. Capital punishment is not applied in a spirit of revenge. Who is there to revenge? The family of the victim have no power to
revenge the death of their relative. Society must protect itself against the murderer and must, by using certain methods, render it impossible for that man to commit a second murder.
Now, if we are to follow out some of the social programmes of reformers, we shall have to begin with every child and see that it is trained in such a way that it will not become a criminal. That is what I assume our schools and churches are trying to do to-day with the children of all classes-teaching them to be moral, to obey the law, to be good citizens. But in spite of all these beneficent agencies, men and women coming from What might be considered good homes fall into evil ways and commit various crimes leading up to murder. Who is to determine whether this child or that is defective until it has done something which demonstrates that it is sub-normal? I do argue that nothing should be done in a collective way to improve our social life, I am ready to support any agency to that end, but I submit that if you remove all the penalties and punishments for crime you remove every deterrent against wrong-doing, and if you remove capital punishment, my judgment is that you will have many more murders, because if a man is inclined to commit murder-and I am speaking of deliberate cold-blooded murder, not of an act arising out of passion-and he is conscious that he will not have to surrender his life but will be committed to the penitentiary, he knows that inside of a few years by submitting to the prison discipline and building up a record for good behaviour he will regain his freedom, that man I say will not be deterred so much in his actions as if he knows that upon conviction for murder he will forfeit his life. There can be no deterrent equal to the forfeiture of a man's life, and any person who argues differently has, I submit, lost sight of one of the fundamental characteristics of human nature. A man will give everything to preserve his life, and if capital punishment does not deter him his case is hopeless.
Since the war closed we have had a series of the most unprovoked, deliberate, coldblooded murders that have ever disgraced civilization.

Does not the hon.
member think that the reason for such murders is that the war itself was simply an utter disregard for human life on a large scale?

I tthink there may be a great deal in what the hon. member says.
Capital Punishment

We looked upon the taking of human life during the war with a good deal of indifference as compared with our attitude in peace, and it may be that a good many of these bandits were closer up to the fighting line and have carried into civil life the practices of war. But take the cities of this continent, you find men organized in gangs who for a few paltry dollars do not hesitate to shoot down people. Such men are simply mankilling tigers, and it is not safe to allow them to be at large.

Does the hon. member
think that I am proposing that the mankilling tiger shall run loose?

No, but I am pointing
out that the resolution means that he would ultimately get out.
What	resolution?

The	resolution before us,
I am pointing out that if you do away with capital punishment-
There	is no resolution before the House. There is a bill before the House.
Well, call it a bill.
There is no such proposal.

All right; I stand corrected-it is a bill that is before the House- not a resolution; and the bill is to abolish capital punishment and give the murderer a chance to go into the penitentiary for a few years and get out again.

Who says that? Do you
say that?

My hon. friend knows very well that while the penalty may be life imprisonment there is hardly a case where a man remains in the penitentiary until his death. The clemency of the Crown is sought by his relatives and by societies such as my hon. friend speaks for, which will get up petitions signed by the yard, asking for clemency for this man and for that. So that after a few years in the penitentiary, with reasonably good conduct-that is, if he does not run amuck and kill somebody else-the convicted man is released. Has the time spent in penitentiary reformed him? Has it made him a good citizen? Is he likely to be a saner and better man when he comes out than when he went in? I do not think so. If he has criminal instincts, inherited, as my hon. friend suggests, and developed by environment, they are certainly not removed by life in the penitentiary, where he is herded entirely with [Mr. Hocken.l
criminals and (is not subject to the beneficent influence of decent society around him as he is when he is out of prison.
I think it is a very great mistake for us even to discuss a question of this kind in the House at this time, for if ever in the history of Canada it was necessary to bring before the criminal population of the country the fact that there is a real penalty and that for murder the penalty is forfeiture of life, that time is now. If this thing is a disease, do you not think steps should be taken to discover it before it breaks out in that murderous form? And if every man who is a criminal or betrays criminal instincts is to be treated as a subject for hospital, then we had better get to work and build hospitals in every county. If you are going to house under detention every defective and every feeble-minded person-because you will have to do that if you want to guard against the development of the criminal instinct in those who are .defective or feebleminded-then you must have institutions in practically every county in the Dominion of Canada.
I believe, Sir, in doing everything that can possibly be done to instruct the youth of this country in the penalties for offences as well as' in the satisfaction of doing right. I am not altogether satisfied that our universities and our whole educational system are upon the right basis. I think a good deal more might be done in the way of educating the children to-day so that they will grow up not only to know that it is wrong to com-
9 p.m. mit crime, but also to understand that if you want to live a decent, a good, a happy life, they must do right. The thing to do is not to tell boys and girls that they must not do this and must not do that. The thing to do is to teach them what they ought to do because it is right and keep them busy doing right. I am not sure that our schools are doing that as effectively as they might. At all events you will not make any progress in the elimination of murder within this country by removing the one penalty that is best calculated to deter the criminal from that offence.
Mr. JOS. T. SHAW (West Calgary): Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) is to be congratulated on having presented to the House in a very definite and clear-cut way the argument against capital punishment. I think he is further to be congratulated on having eliminated from his consideration the question of sentimentality: he has endeavoured, and,
I think, successfully, to present the argument in the light of cold and calculated reason.

Capital Punishment
I agree with the hon. member for Brandon <Mr. Forke)) that if any member of this House were asked to draw the bolt which might drop some unfortunate individual into eternity, he would hesitate to undertake the task. But we must not forget that as a parliament, we constitute the hangman of the nation. Upon us rests the responsibility; we cannot shelve it off on some mortal whom we may delegate to draw the bolt on a particular individual. The responsibility rests collectively and individually upon this parliament, upon every preceding parliament, and upon every parliament, for continuing in existence this method-I think this barbarous method-of extinguishing life. So I say it is a solemn and a serious matter and one which should engage our very earnest consideration.
It cannot be denied that punishment by the state has, generally speaking, two objects to serve: First, to punish the individual, and, in cases other than those in which the capital sentence is pronounced and carried out, to reform that individual, and, secondly, to deter those under temptation from committing similar offences. Now, in examining this question I think it is well for us to determine on whom the onus lies of establishing whether or not this system should be continued. I venture to say, and I do not believe there is a single member of this House who will contradict me, that the onus rests upon the advocates of capital punishment to establish beyond a doubt that that is the system which will deter the commission of similar offences. Let there be no mistake about that, because I want definitely to charge the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and those who think with him that the responsibility is theirs to establish to the satisfaction of this House the necessity for the continuance of this system of punishment.
What are the essentials that must be established? It must be established, first of all, whether or not capital punishment is a deterrent; secondly, whether it is the sole deterrent, and, thirdly, whether it is indispensable. Those are the three factors that must be established before this parliament can be justified in continuing to act as the hangman of the nation. When we commence to discuss the deterrent value of capital punishment-because so far as the person who is executed is concerned that is the only substantial question with which we are concerned -we enter at once into a field of surmise and of conjecture. I venture to say that no one can distinctly state what the deterrent value of capital punishment is. If you take a look at the figures you will find, for example, in the United States, where in some states they 83
have capital punishment and in other life imprisonment, and where they have gone from one variety to the other and back-that there is substantially no difference in the figures. I believe that if the figures prove anything they prove that there is little difference in the result, whether life imprisonment or the supreme penalty of the law is exacted.
Realizing his responsibility in this matter, the Minister of Justice has given us certain figures with which to establish the contention that capital punishment is essential,, and, I suppose, to prove that it is a deterrent. Well, now, let us take his figures. He compares the three Anglo-Saxon countries, the United States, England and Canada. He shows that the number of murders committed in the United States is much larger proportionately than those committed in Canada and that in Canada the number is proportionately smaller than it is even in England. We have capital punishment in all these places. Does it prove what the Minister sets out to prove? Not at all. What it does prove is that if we are to believe reports that come to us from time to time from the United States, it is not the severity of punishment that counts as the deterrent factor; it is the certainty of punishment that counts; and so I venture to say that the figures given in that connection by the minister do not in any sense at all establish the object for which I presume he gave them.
Then he gave us certain other figures. He found himself under the necessity of going into the field of war for the purpose of producing some figures. He tells us that the Australian troops were not subject to the death penalty in the ease of desertion, that at the outset of the war no such rule prevailed in the Canadian corps, but that among the English troops the death penalty was always exacted for desertion. He produced no figures in that connection but gave the statement of some writer, and we do not know whether that gentleman produced any figures or not. But the situation is altogether different. That was not a society of men organized for purposes of peace. That was a society of men organized for purposes of war-a most unusual and most unlikely situation from which to extract figures to prove that capital punishment was ' desirable. In the next place I venture to put before the House the situation with regard to a young soldier who has been charged with desertion. Just imagine his situation. Here he is, on the one hand, facing danger and the possibility of death. We know nothing with regard to his physical condition, we know nothing with regard to his mental condition, and under these circumstances, fac-

Capital Punishment

ing an unknown future and perhaps overcome and losing control of himself, he deserts the army and goes into the back areas. Now surely the minister, if there is anything in his argument at all, could have gathered from some other course some arguments that would have justified him in saying that capital punishment is in deed and in fact a deterrent to the commission of murder by other people. I want in this connection to read just a short statement made by the same gentleman from whom the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) quoted this afternoon:
Here, on the bare plane of justice and expediency we might let our argument rest, in the full confidence that a system which violated those canons of civilized living cannot much longer be endured. But the problem has a deeper aspect. The whole upward struggle of humanity is an effort to realize and consecrate new human values, a nobler range of feeling. It is not enough to "let the ape and tiger die"-the one must be supplanted by the man, "looking before and after;" the other by the finer feelings which are embodied in the humanitarian sentiment to which I have previously referred. What, then, can be said for a system of punishment which keeps reviving in us the sentiments of hatred and cruelty which are our worst inheritance from our animal forbears? We aim to inculcate a respect for human life by ourselves showing our contempt for human life. Some of the most tragic effects of this procedure have been noticed in an earlier part of this paper. But there is no way of estimating the more general and subtle demoralization which it produces. It is probably no exaggeration to say that every execution is accompanied by a distinct lowering of the moral tone of the entire community. Its only redeeming feature is the horror it excites in the more sensitive natures. To the much larger number, to whom it presents itself as an act of vengeance, a gratification of primitive blood-lust, it is an unmixed moral evil.
May I commend this further statement to the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) ?
From this point of view, there is little to choose between the various methods that are mercifully employed to inflict the death penalty. The guillotine, the hangman's rope, the electric chair, the lethal chamber-all are equally revolting to humane feeling; all become equally sensational, all are equally cruel. Indeed, the cold blooded, deliberate killing of the criminal by the state, by whatever method,, is the refinement of cruelty, and the victim dies a hundred deaths before he is mercifully relieved by the actual extinction of life and feeling.
Further on he stages:
It is an over-simplified view of a complex social phenomenon that makes it possible for us to believe that a grave menace can be seriously modified by the processes of legal justice. I am sure that many who seem to favour capital punishment will agree that such a phenomenon as the persistence and increase of the murder rate in our civilization has a profounder cause than the inefficiency of our system of criminal justice and that if we are to eradicate or even appreciably modify the evil, we must go to the roo(t of the matter, find the deep-lying causes, and deal with them. It is not the murderer, but murder, that is our enemy.
