The primitive method of striking blindly, in impotent rage, at the life of the offender has had its day, but it still obscures our vision as to the real nature of our problem.

I say that in this matter we. cannot rest our vote upon a matter of mere sentiment. We cannot rest it upon a mere matter of conscientious feeling, however sincere that may be, and so I ask each and every member of the House: Are we to leave this House to-night with this parliament continuing as the hangman of the nation, placing our judgment only upon mere sentiment or upon a mere conscientious conviction, however sincere it may be, when in fact and in reason we should usher in a day when justice shall become humane and when humanitarianism shall become wise.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
This subject has been up almost every session since I have entered the House. It has always been received by hon. members with interest, carefully treated and disposed of. One cannot help taking an interest in it no matter how frequently it is presented, but I stand to confess I would take infinitely more interest if I felt that our present practice of inflicting the death penalty were in any real danger of being abandoned. If I felt that we were at all near any imminent peril in that regard my interest in the subject would be quickened in the extreme. I am opposed, resolutely opposed, to the motion.	[DOT]
One needs to examine first, what is the present law and practice. Under the law of Canada, as of Britain, as of many other countries the most advanced in the world, the death penalty is inflictable for murder, inflictable here also for treason, and as well for the crime of rape. I do not propose to discuss the wisdom of the law in relation to the latter two, because the whole principle at stake is more simply discussed when referred merely to the first.
In practice the death penalty is actually inflicted when murder is first proven to have taken place, and murder under our Code has so narrow and clear a definition that it must be atrocious and cold-blooded to come within the terms of the law.
But after the jury's verdict and the sentence there is vested in the Department of Justice a power of review, and it is only a fair statement of the practice to say that any circumstances that go to show the lack of apprecia-' tion, the mental inferiority of the accused, even far removed from actual insanity, or other circumstances of a strongly mitigating character, operate to relieve the victim from the extreme penalty. So that we are left in the position, in the actual practice of. our law, that the most atrocious cold-blooded instances alone are followed through to capital punishment.

Capital Punishment
The question before us is, should this penalty be done away with in such cases? First of all,
I will seek to remove, if I can, some of the, what seems to me, mere confusion that has been advanced by way of argument in support of the motion. It is said that after all crime is latent, that it is a social growth. Crime is not, we are told, so much the actual positive, wilful wtong-doing blamable on the perpetrator as it is the outgrowth of bad, social conditions, inborn sin, wrong social relations, or perhaps the result of some blood legacy in the offender, for all of which he personally is not responsible- I am ready to give some weight to these allegations. I am ready to assume, for the sake of argument, if for nothing else, that crime is pretty much the outgrowth of imperfect social relations and conditions. I am ready to admit, for the sake of argument if for no other reason, that the man of criminal instinct is pretty much the victim of heredity. I do not know how far those contentions are true; I believe they are true to some extent. But wherein do these things affect the case? They go to show that we certainly should seek to improve our social conditions, that the first object of legislation should be the amelioration of our social relations- It goes to show as well that we should do what we perhaps are not doing, that we should take more practical steps-to improve the conditions of heredity under which the child is born. I am ready to agree that those conclusions follow from the hypothesis laid down by certain hon. members whom I have heard.
But do any other conclusions follow? After we have done our best in these regards, criminals still remain. The problem of the criminal is still with us. The obligation to protect society is still here. What are we going to do? Are we bound to say that because underlying causes are there, perhaps far more powerful than the wilful, responsible inclinations of the accused, on that account we should not follow through the most atrocious crimes to capital punishment? It is just as logical to say that we should do away with the whole system of punishment altogether. It is just as logical to say that no offence against society should be punished at all, that our whole penal code should be swept away. When one states the case in that form, it removes altogether, at least from my mind, what is sought to be erected on this theory of unsound social conditions as an argument against the application of the extreme penalty to the perpetrator of capital crime. Punishment is a practical necessity. The history of all ages shows that we 83i
must inflict it. It has to be done, or we cannot hold organized society together.
Let us come therefore to what is the appropriate, or I had better say, the effective, punishment for the true purposes of all punishment, as applicable to that class of crime which I first of all described. What are the true purposes of punishment? One of them was stated by the hon. gentleman who has just spoken to be vengeance against the accused. I disagree with him. I do not think that is any object of legal penalty at all. The real object is, as he says, two-fold. It is first to provide a deterrent against crime, to the perpetrator, and to others; and secondly the object is reformative as regards the accused. Both are sought to be served by the whole philosophy of our penal system. In the minor grades of crime, the second takes a very important place. As the grades of crime become more gross, more abhorrent, more heinous, more atrocious, then the first must become more and more important. The blacker the crime, the more perilous it is to society, the more overwhelming must be the weight given the deterrent effect of the punishment in deciding what the punishment, shall be. The blackest of all crimes of course are those for which the capital penalty is allotted. It is undoubtedly therefore true that in those cases the consideration which we must keep mostly before us is the deterrent effect of any punishment we apply. I am free to admit that punishment should be no greater than is sufficient to bring about the maximum of deterrent effect, no matter how heinous the crime. It may be that in earlier centuries for offences of a minor, or what one might call a medium character, punishments unnecessary for deterrent effect, and inappropriate in every respect were imposed. But before I would castigate too freely our ancestors in this respect, I would desire to understand just what were all the circumstances of those times. I fancy if all their conditions were understood we would conclude that they were, perhaps, not in mental stature or in political judgment very far our inferiors. But we are judging now of the times in which we live, and before we conclude to apply, in place of the punishment of death, the punishment of imprisonment, or any other punishment for the offence of him, who, in cold blood and for the motives that virtually always animate a murderer slaughters his fellow-man, we want to know what that punishment is going to prove by way of a deterrent, because if we are not sure of its efficacy to this paramount end, we
Capital Punishment

shall probably be merely submitting the innocent to a fate from which the guilty have been relieved.
I have heard some figures presented by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), for the purpose of establishing that the experience of civilization had shown-and he spoke, of course, of the civilization of to-day-that these crimes of the blackest enormity, were deterred best by capital punishment. He advanced two classes of statistics. First he showed that the death penalty had proven the best deterrent in the case of the crime of desertion. His illustrations, are disputed as to their application by the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine). I really could not follow the argument of the hon. member. I know the offence of desertion differs from the offence of murder; but what has that fact to do with the question as to the relative merits of capital and other punishment as deterrents? It has been proven in actual practice that stern necessity compelled the application of one punishment and one alone as effective against the offence of desertion. The deduction from those statistics is plain; it is that that punishment is feared the most, which proves the most effective to prevent-namely the capital penalty.
But the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) brought figures as well to show that, as applied to the offence of murder, the death penalty had proved there also the most effective. He compared the results in the United States, in Canada and in England, and he showed that in Canada and England murders were much the less frequent, in Canada the least frequent of all. The hon. member to my left, says: "Oh, but in all those countries they have capital punishment, and the only difference is that in the United States the certainty . of the penalty is not so great as it is in Canada and in England." But the United States has experimented with other penalties for many years. The United States to-day have some states, I do not know7 exactly how many-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Eleven.

-eleven states to-day where capital punishment is not applied, and in some others-I could name one or two now-they suspended the application of this punishment and tried other experiments for a time, but the awful results showed that they had to return to the sterner penalty. No, the United States is not in the position that Canada is in. There, they have asylums for murderers, which we do not have, and because they have those asylums, murder there is more 
rampant than it is here. It is quite true that the certainty of the penalty is even more important than its adequacy; and the conclusion is that, no matter what the penalty, w'e should not relax our efforts to make its imposition certain, and it is to the glory of this Dominion that we have not so relaxed. To this circumstance we attribute in considerable degree the paucity of capital crime which we enjoy. But we cannot deny that it is due also in very great degree to the fact that rigidly and sternly we have adhered consistently to the death penalty, that we can boast of our comparisons as against the United States.
On other occasions, I have investigated these statistics myself, and I believe many more could be adduced to support the contention of the Minister of Justice, that when one places the death penalty against other punishments and compares them as deterrents, the death penalty has a place all by itself. Life is sweet to everyone, and there is something, I suppose, of the coward in us all. But there is no man who so values his life, and who feels so poignantly the coward's fear of death as the fiend who goes out, for his owm gain or to appease some selfish animosity or lust, to slaughter his fellow man. Such a creature fears death himself infinitely more than does his manly brother who holds sacred human life.
But if we did not have statistics, and if we did not have some experience with the criminal, surely our knowledge of human nature in general would teach us that nothing will stay the hand of the man with murder in his soul like the fear of death. One has to put oneself in the position of the intended victim or one close and dear to that victim to know just what the situation is. We are all inclined to have some sympathy for the unfortunate creature who has to face the ghastly tragedy of the hangman's noose, and as time passes from the murderous event, we are likely to become more and more sentimental or sympathetic. But let every hon. member place himself in the position, say, of the father of the home who finds that a fiend in the form of man, to appease his lust or his love of gold, has broken into his home and slaughtered wife or child. Would he feel that any sufficient deterrent would be held out to others if it were the law of Canada, that such a fiend should be kept for the rest of his life at the expense of the state, and the public taxed to reform him? No, the hope of reform, that element or phase of the purpose of punishment does not take any very important place when we come to deal with

those who take the life of their fellows. There, the deterrent element must he held supreme. All other elements amount to little. I for one am profoundly convinced, so profoundly that, J am sure nothing, even infinitely stronger in the way of argument than anything J have heard to-day. could move me, that the very security of society, all that we hold dear, depends upon maintaining strong and stern the death penalty against the most vicious *of all crimes.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to associate myself with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) in the remarks which he has just made with reference to the bill that is before the Plouse. I think every hon. member of the House feels the great responsibility which rests upon him in even pronouncing an opinion with reference to a matter affecting human life. I am sure all of us are viewing this question from the point of view of the value of human life, and what will make most for the preservation of human life, and, may I add, of innocent human life. If I believed that the bill which the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) has introduced, would make for the preservation of innocent human life, would make in the end for a greater saving of human life, as is his object in proposing to substitute a sentence for life instead of the death penalty, I would vote with him. But I believe to the contrary; I believe that the deterrent effect of the death penalty, having regard to human society as it is constituted and to human character as we know it, is in the end to protect innocent people from the murderous assaults that may be made upon them by some of the individuals who compose our human society.
If I had had occasion to address the House on this subject some years ago, perhaps, I might have spoken a little more in the vein in which my hon. friend from East Calgary has spoken to-day. Since that time, in the short period within which my colleagues and I have been entrusted with the added responsibility of having to advise His Excellency whether or not the law shall take its course in cases of murder, I have had to consider, as my colleagues have also had to consider, and as my right hon. friend opposite and his colleagues when in office had very carefully to consider, in the case of every murder that has come before the cabinet for consideration, whether or not human society would be better protected in the long run by a sentence for life than by enforcement of the death penalty in case of murder.
Capital Punishment
There is no graver, there is no more serious, there is no more trying duty imposed upon a minister of the Crown than that which he has to exercise in being obliged to advise His Excellency, with respect to every capital case, whether or not the law shall take its course.
There is one factor in our country of which I think account should be taken in passing upon this question. Were capital punishment lightly inflicted, were it a matter of lynching where murder has taken place, we might well pause before consenting to such a course being permissible. But under British law every man, and no man more than one accused of crime, is protected by all the safeguards which human ingenuity has been able to devise for the purpose of ensuring a fair trial. The murderer is brought before a court of justice and there he or his counsel has the right to challenge those selected to serve on the jury until he secures to try him, twelve men whom he believes to be fair and impartial, twelve of his fellow men. Judges have no more desire to see human life ended than have other individuals in the community. There is no judge who in a matter affecting life and death addresses a jury lightly; nor are there any twelve men who compose a jury who view lightly the verdict which they give. But that is not all. After a court has had the facts before it, and after the jury have considered every circumstance very carefully, where they find the circumstances justify the imposition of the death penalty upon a man or woman who has committed murder and the penalty is imposed, the case then comes before His Excellency in Council for consideration. There the facts relevant to every case are reviewed by the cabinet as a whole. The Minister of Justice has the grave responsibility of reviewing the entire evidence; in presenting the matter to his colleagues for consideration he invariably takes into account every extenuating circumstance. Mention has been made to-day of possible mental infirmity and other circumstances of a like nature,-

May I point out to the Prime Minister that neither the judge nor the jury has anything to do with the death penalty. Their business is to find out whether the accused is guilty of the crime. This parliament, how'ever, has to do with the penalty.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think I
understand the force of what my hon. friend is saying. Certainly the judge and jury do not execute the death penalty; but they realize that the result of their actions may determine whether or not a particular individual may have to suffer the penalty of death. They are the judges of the facts, and if
Capital Punishment

they find that the act is one of premeditated murder, the taking of a human life, they know that the result of such a verdict will be that the murderer will be hanged.

It would be a miscarriage
of justice if they did not render a verdict according to the evidence. The judge has no responsibility in the matter; in imposing the death penalty he simply carries out the law of the country- Consequently the responsibility rests upon the people who make the law.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I appreciate
that fact. The same kind of responsibility rests upon every member of the government in advising His Excellency whether or not the law must take its course. What I am trying to point out is that it is not a matter of quick judgment, it is not a matter of hasty decision, it is not a matter of chance as to whether an individual under British law will be hanged or not. One charged with the crime of murder is likely to be hanged only after a large number of conscientious men, feeling gravely the responsibility which they are called upon to exercise, sincerely believe that the act which has been committed was a premeditated murder of some innocent human being. If I believed that in the long run, more innocent human lives would be saved by permitting those who are guilty of murder to serve a life sentence than is the case under executions, I would support my hon. friend. I view the whole question from the standpoint of the preservation of human life in our society. What course will most effectively save innocent human lives? I believe that the death penalty does have a deterrent effect, and I feel that more strongly because of the knowledge I have of the number of capital cases that have come before the cabinet in the short time in which this government has been in office, where we have had before us the circumstances of every individual case of murder that has taken place. These cases have revealed clearly the fact that the men who have been found guilty of murder have premeditated the crime for the most part from motives of lust or avarice Were they and others like them to suffer only life imprisonment for their crimes, knowing the psychological effect exercised upon . other minds and natures when such crimes are committed, I believe that the number of murders would vastly increase once the death penalty were abolished. For that reason I am opposed to the principle of the bill.

Has the Prime Minister
examined the figures in this regard in relation to other countries that have abolished

the death penalty? Upon what ground rests his belief that the abolition of capital punishment would lead to an increase in the number of murders that are being committed?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
So far as
figures are concerned, it has often been said that statistics can be made to prove anything, and I believe that to be largely true. Only last evening I was speaking regarding this very matter with a gentleman who represents a large number of religious organizations. He mentioned to me the fact, which has been cited this evening, that in some of the American states where the death penalty was removed the number of murders considerably increased. In one state where / referendum was held the people themselves because of the increased number of murders that were being committed, repealed the law which had removed the death penalty.

That is the only one
known.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
No, I would
not say it was the only one. However, I judge this matter, as one is obliged to judge everything, in the light of our knowledge of human nature and in the light of all known facts and circumstances,. I can assure my hon. friend that if he had the responsibility which I have where a criminal is to be hanged, of being obliged as President of the Council to sign the recommendation to His Excellency to allow the law to take its course, he would doubly feel the solemnity of standing in this House and advising that hanging should be continued as the penalty for murder. Because I have that responsibility I am the more anxious to exercise it in the light only of what I honestly believe will make most for the preservation of human life in this Dominion. I do believe that the retention of the death penalty, surrounded as it is in Canada by all the safeguards which British justice affords, will serve more effectively to afford protection to members of our human society, than any change in the law which would substitute the' life sentence for capital punishment.

One word of explanation.
The question I asked the Prime Minister had nothing to do with any argument for or against the death penalty. I did not ask the question from that angle. I asked it to point out the fact that neither the judge, nor the jury, nor the minister who afterwards considers the petition for a reprieve is responsible for the death penalty; they are simply carrying out the law as enacted by parliament. That was the idea behind my question.

Capital Punishment

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I quite understand my hon. friend. I would add to what he says,-that they are also responsible for the possible consequences of removing the death penalty and substituting some other penalty therefor.
Certainly.

Mr. Speaker, with a full sense of
my responsibility as a member of the government and with a full appreciation of the position taken by my chief (Mr. Mackenzie King) and by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), and of the particularly able argument of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), I still feel bound to adhere to the opinions which I have formed upon the question of capital punishment after long years of practice in the criminal courts defending men charged with murder.
The question has been ably canvassed today, without any sentimentality. I think we need offer no apology for supporting the bill now before us. Some of the ablest men in the world have been in favour of the abolition of the death penalty: statesmen, such as Bright and Gladstone; jurists such as Grotius and Bentham; reformers such as Osborne, and Robespierre immortalized himself and practically overcame the evils of a life time by his eloquent address in opposition to the death penalty. Highly civilized nations both past and present have abolished capital punishment; for instance, the people of Athens, and of Holland,-nations that rank high in the history of the world. So that to-day the abolition of the death penalty is an appropriate subject for debate.
I agree entirely with the right hon. leader of the opposition that there can be only two grounds for inflicting punishment on criminals: first, the protection of society; second, the reformation of the individual. I believe that punishment plays but a very minor part in the prevention of crime. The scientific study of crime is exceedingly interesting. As the Minister of Justice pointed out, crime varies in different localities and among different people, and at different seasons of the year and under differing economic conditions. In our country we find that crime increases during migration and diminishes when people are tied to home and kindred.
In olden times the criminal code of England was as bloody as is the code of Japan to-day, but although the death penalty applied to 147 crimes, such as highway robbery and sheep stealing, and thousands of people were executed
every year, still capital punishment did not have the effect intended and crime continued. Making allowance for the advance of civilization which the right hon. gentleman in his closely reasoned argument referred to, it has been shown that capital punishment does not prevent crime. Hon. gentlemen have pointed out that after the war murder and other crimes of violence increased in this country, clearly demonstrating that the death penalty is not a preventive. I believe that those who commit murder are not deterred by any penalty, however severe.
The sources of crime are manifold. Many murders are committed under the influence of drink or of narcotics, and when men become angry and lose control of themselves they act regardless of the consequences. Then again some murderers are mentally incompetent. Take the case of the recent bank robbery in Montreal to which my hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) referred. Those men probably knew what the penalty would be, but still they did not hesitate to commit murder. So I do not think that hon. members have succeeded in proving that capital punishment prevents crime. There is no doubt that it is a deterrent. But the question is: Is it a greater deterrent than life imprisonment?
In many states of the union, particulary in the state of Michigan, homicide is punished with life imprisonment. The man who assassinated President McKinley could have done so in Detroit, and would have been subject to life imprisonment; but he followed his victim to Buffalo, and suffered the death penalty for his crime. But what appears to me to be the strongest argument against capital punishment is this. The state demands from the murderer an absolute, definite price-his life. Before the state is entitled to demand that penalty it should prove beyond all peradventure that the accused is guilty. Law is not an exact science-criminal law least of all. Take a trial for murder, the chances are that knowing the lawyer for the defence you may be fairly certain what the verdict of the jury will be. There are differences in human nature. An inexperienced lawyer may select his jury carelessly and the chances are that the man he is defending will go to the gallows, whereas if the same prisoner had been defended by a lawyer of wider experience who had a better knowledge of the law and of human nature, with perhaps a different judge presiding, the accused man might have been acquitted. That is exactly the practical working of it.

There is a judge and
jury, but there must also be witnesses.
Capital Punishment

Oh yes, there must be witnesses, and there is one of the great difficulties. Evidence is not always reliable. Circumstantial evidence is not reliable, direct evidence probably less so. We have had a number of cases where men have been wrongfully convicted. I happen to hold in my hand a clipping I took from the Ottawa Journal last year just about the time this question came up; it is typical of What is occurring and has been occurring in various parts of the world. It says, referring to a United States case:	'
Innocent man was serving a life sentence. Youth confesses to murder of policeman for which other man sent down. Prisoner always held that he was innocent. When told he would be freed, McKinney said he always believed he would get out.
Had that taken place in a state where capital punishment was provided for, the innocent man would have been hanged; as it was, he had been sentenced to life imprisonment. I have here also, cut out about the same time, a picture of a young Greek who had been convicted and sentenced to a long term of imprisonment in the state of New York. He maintained his innocence, and after a long hunt over the United States, away in distant California they located a man who confessed that it was he who had committed the crime. There was a ease like that in England, which every lawyer in this House is no doubt familiar with, the case of Adolf Beck. Adolf Beck was a Swedish engineer, and one night when he went out to buy a newspaper he was accused by a woman of having swindled her. He protested and said, "I will hand you over to the police if you do not leave me alone." He was taken to jail, tried, convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for five or seven years ,all the time protesting his innocence. He applied repeatedly to the Home Secretary for consideration of his case, and finally after serving, I think, four years of his term, was released. Shortly afterwards he was again arrested, charged with practically the same crime, and again sent to prison.
It showed that he was not a good boy. .

What about his
victim and what about the victim's family?
Capital Punishment

Well, the suffering of the family is nothing to what this man suffers But in any case, why should we bring the state down to the same
10 p m. plane; why should we impose torture upon the man in the cell because the family of the victim suffer? Will it. relieve the family of their suffering to know that another man is day by day going through hell waiting for the gallows? In many states of the United States the death penalty has been abolished. In some it has been reinstated; that is a matter of opinion. I do believe that the death penalty was instituted because it seemed to be an appropriate penalty. The idea was not altogether the protection of society; it was more in accordance with the theory of "an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth"; that if a man takes life it is appropriate that he should lose his own. The code carrying that provision, however, seems not to go the full distance.
If you are going to execute the murderer, are you going to execute the man who attempts murder? Our code says no. Why not? If the man who attempted murder had the determination to kill, and was prevented from doing it, if it is necessary to protect, society why do you not execute the man who attempts murder? No; that is on the statute book; it has dragged down behind the old appeal of retribution and revenge.
I still hold the opinion I held some years ago, that capital punishment is not a deterrent, that it has within it that which might inflict a terrible wrong that could never be repaired. I do not think the state should leave itself in that position where there is a danger of that awful wrong being inflicted. If society is not protected more by capital punishment than by some other system, if we can prevent these odious executions that are taking place in our land and that are not necessary, then I think Canada will be marching forward, and will have struck down one more of the barbaric institutions that have come down to us from the past. I have no hesitation in voting whole-heartedly for the resolution brought in by my hon. friend.
Mr. A. M. CARMICHAEL (Kindersley). I have listened to many hon. members from this quarter of the House advance their views in reference to this bill, and I think without exception they have all followed along the same line of thought. I do not know whether I am of a very perverse nature or not, but I find I am not in agreement with my compatriots in this comer. I do not find my mind running along the same line of thought as theirs.
Listening to the debate I have been wondering where we get our authority for capital punishment. We have had references made by different members to Canadian custom; we have had statistics quoted from American practices; we have had some take us across the water and quote the British traditions and practice; but I have been led to ask myself the question: Are any of these countries really authoritative in their practices? Can we base our custom on what any one of these countries do? And I have been led to run my mind back to the written record we have of the first murder that happened some six thousand years ago. At that time Cain slew Abel-the first murder we have record of. Now the only punishment that was meted out to Cain was a mark placed upon his forehead. I do not think he was given life imprisonment; he was allowed to run at large. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that was a deterrent to crime, because we find that as civilization rolled on century after century for some six thousand or more years, there was a law instituted against murder. That law came to us not through a person that was revengeful, not through a person that was barbaric in nature; that law came to us through that great leader Moses who, the record tells us, was the meekest man in all the earth; and it did not seem to just fit in with my ideas to hear this practice of capital punishment classified as being barbaric and as something that, was so hideous when it was handed out to civilization by a man of the character of Moses. And, Mr. Speaker, he did not originate the practice. The capital punishment idea was given to man by the One who created mankind. On Mount Sinai the Divine decree was: Thou shalt not kill. Now if any man or any woman dares to take upon himself or herself the right to violate that Divine decree and go out and kill, it is right that they should be subject to the penalty that was instituted at the time that decree was given.

Will the hon. member allow me a question. He has referred to the first murderer, Cain. Does he know why the law put a mark on Cain, as set forth in the Scriptures? I may be questioning the hon. member too closely. If I remember aright, it was that nobody should slay him.

I am prepared to
accept the interpretation of the hon. member.

Not the interpretation, the fact.
Capital Punishment

I am dealing now some fifteen hundred years this side of that mark. We find that that mark did not deter murders, and that was the reason why a different method was given by the Creator. As I stated, the penalty for taking life was that life should be taken. If a man or a woman took the life of a human being the Creator said that he or she should pay the penalty with his or her life, and that law was given to us by the meek man, Moses. Now, generally speaking, we can say that our Canadian law is based upon Bible law, at least in a great many respects. For instance, in reference to our marriage custom, if we wish to define the relationships in marriage we go back to Bible law and base our practice on what is said there. I am rather sorry to state that in reference to divorce we also go back to the Mosaic law. We jump over the New Testament teaching and the prohibitory legislation enacted in the New Testament, and go back to the Mosaic law in respect to divorce, and we in parliament sanction many cases of divorce that we should not. Now in reference to the taking of life, are we going to leave behind the Mosaic practice and follow the New Testament teaching, which, of course, we know prohibits the taking of life. The New Testament teaching I realize is entirely different from the old Mosaic law. The New Testament teaching is one of loving your enemies, it is one of turning the other cheek, it is one of resisting not evil; but, Mr. Speaker, I wish to state right here that there is no nation that is Christian in the full sense of the word. Christian means Christ-like, and there is no nation that is Christ-like in every detail. Nations are not wholly and completely Christian, while individuals in them may be and are. Therefore if our nations are not Christian or Christ-like we must revert to the Mosaic law to govern ourselves in regard to crime and its punishment.
Now what do we find present conditions to be? We find murders prevailing, bank robberies, forgeries, conspiracies, wars and such like. If we had in our country such conditions as New Testament teaching outlines we would not have these things existing, and there would be no need for capital punishment. But we do not find these conditions prevailing; we find that man will go out and take the life of his fellow man. I recall that the mover of the bill advocates a term of imprisonment as punishment for the crime of taking life. I was led to think, Mr. Speaker, of an instance that happened about a year ago over in England. I remember the

case quite well. It was about the time this bill was on our order paper last year, but it did not come up for discussion, so that no argument was advanced pro or con. The particular case I refer to was that of a young married couple in England. The wife was about 25 years of age, and her husband was probably five or six years older. Another man entered upon the scene and had covetous desires towards this particular wife, and he and the wife plotted together to get rid of the legitimate husband. It was a premeditated cold-blooded plan. They arranged that on a particular night, when the husband and wife would be returning from the theatre, this second man should murder the husband. The plan was carried out and the husband was murdered. The wife professed great sorrow for the death of her husband and he was buried. But evidence was adduced to show who the real murderers were. They were brought to the bar of justice. They were given a fair and just trial and were condemned to death. Both were hanged. I was led to ask myself the question if, instead of the capital penalty being imposed, these people had been imprisoned for life, what would have been the effect on society?
In addition to that, I would like to point out the fact that our prison life to-day is something that is not to be dreaded. I listened to a lecture in this city last year by General Hughes, outlining to us the conditions of prison life as it is experienced at Kingston. He told us the size of the cell and stated that they had clean linen there if not every day, every other day. They had running water in their rooms. In fact I was led to think, when he was outlining the conditions of the prisoner in the cell, that the conditions were much more enviable than the conditions of our homesteaders on the prairies. Now, realizing that the conditions were such, if this particular man and the wife, these murderers, were placed under such conditions, would that be sufficient punishment for them? Would that act as a deterrent to others and prevent them from planning and hatching similar crimes. Indeed it would not. These people would remain in prison for perhaps ten years, possibly only five; then public sympathy would be worked up in their favour and they would be given their liberty. The chances are that they would then get married, and their example would be a great incentive to the commission of similar crimes. If I were to look at the case from a sentimental point of view I would feel like abolishing the death penalty; but when I consider it from the viewpoint of my duty towards mankind and towards

Capital Punishment
society in general, I do not feel that, under present conditions, we would be wise in abolishing the death penalty.

The
subject matter of the motion of my hon. friend from East Calgary (Mr. Irvine) is of very much greater importance than many of the matters that are considered by this House. It is inevitable that sentiment should very largely enter into the consideration of a question of this character. I regret very much, Mr. Speaker, that I have only heard a portion of the addresses given by hon. members on this question. I was not aware that the matter was coming up to-day and was absent for a time from the House. But after listening to the arguments presented so far as I have heard them, I think the only substantial argument advanced against the proposal of the hon. member for East Calgary is that it is a deterrent to the commission of the crime of murder-that by the imposition of the death penalty an influence is exercised upon some to deter them from the perpetration of the crime of murder. I cannot agree with the soundness of that argument. I doubt if there are any people who have committed the heinous crime of murder who have calculated for a second before the act, the consequences of the crime they were about to commit. It is a curious thing how psychological influences operate upon the minds of men. It is a fact, I think acknowledged beyond dispute, that a crime committed, even the crime of murder, may in itself be an incentive to other crimes. We know for instance that we have such things as epidemics of suicide. I recall several instances of that, where the mere fact of a person jumping over a bridge into a river had the effect psychologically of inducing other people to do the same thing. The same holds true in respect to murder, and that is one of the factors that operate, and no sentence of hanging, or the death penalty in any form, will be a deterrent in that case.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member states that a man who commits murder does not consider the consequence of his act. Does he not think that men sometimes do not commit murder because they' calculate what the consequences of their act will be?

While the argument of my hon. friend might have some weight, I do not think it has a great deal of weight. But my support of my hon. friend from East Calgary rests upon other grounds mainly. I think it is a dreadful thing, Mr. Speaker, to have a miscarriage of justice. My hon.
friend the Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray) gave some very illuminating evidence in his * address to-night on this question-perhaps the most pertinent evidence that has been presented in the discussion of the whole matter in the House this afternoon. There is not only a possibility of a miscarriage of justice through an innocent man being condemned, but there is also the possibility of a guilty man getting off scot free, because the penalty of death would be imposed if he were convicted. And how does that arise? It arises mainly through appeals to the emotions of the jury, and through appeals to the sensibilities of the public; which also re-act on a jury when the case comes to trial, after the crime is committed, the person charged with it is incarcerated. The case is one of public discussion, and preconceived notions often exist in the minds of juries before they go into the jury box, which notions, notwithstanding their oath when they enter that box, notwithstanding how honest they may be, are bound to influence their judgment when they come to the question of rendering their verdict. I recall an eminent criminal lawyer telling me on one occasion that he had defended more than thirty men charged with murder and that only one of them had been convicted.
A good lawyer.

He was a good lawyer in that line. I know of cases where an appropriate place in the court room was selected for the accused'^ wife, or his children, or his mother, or his relatives, and an appeal made to the sentiments and emotions of the jurymen under these circumstances, a plea that the accused should not be sent to the galloVs. Men sitting in the box, charged with the grave responsibility of deciding whether one of their fellow men should be sent to the gallows or not, give their verdict for acquittal, sometimes when the weight of evidence is strongly against the accused.
That, however, is not the most serious part of the whole matter. There is the possibility that an innocent man may be sent to the gallows. There is the certainty that, in many cases, innocent men have- been sent to the gallows. The Solicitor General (Mr. McMurray) to-night cited cases, not one, but several, where innocent men charged with the crime of murder were convicted and paid the supreme penalty of the law, and it was later discovered that they were innocent. We know of many cases where men have maintained their innocence of the crime when standing upon the very trap that was to send them to
Capital Punishment

eternity. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen), and also the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) have dwelt, I think, in rather an exaggerated way, upon the tremendous suffering, the loss, the feelings of the friends of a person who has been murdered. But there is the reverse side of the picture. I would rather that one hundred men convicted of murder-guilty, if you like- were sent to the penitentiary to expiate their crimes there instead of expiating them on the gallows, than that one innocent man should suffer death through maintenance of the death penalty. That, to my mind, is one of the strongest arguments in favour of a reconsideration of this question. No matter how honestly, how impartially we endeavour to administer justice in respect of, not only this matter, but others, we know that justice sometimes miscarries, and I can imagine nothing that is more to be deplored than this very fact that an innocent man might suffer the supreme penalty of the law for this crime. For those reasons I propose to support the motion of the hon. member for East Calgary.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to say just a few words on this question. I have no expectation but that the motion will be defeated, otherwise I would have prepared myself to speak at greater length than I intend. I am not such a desperate character as the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird), who would take one end of the rope and hang a man on the other end, although I may say that, listening to this discussion, there are times when I would feel almost in favour of widening the scope of hanging. I have heard the argument advanced that hanging has no deterrent. effect. Let me explain lucidly to the House where it has a deterrent effect. I knew well a young man who murdered a man in cold blood in British Columbia. He was imprisoned. He escaped from prison and after escaping he murdered another man. He was recaptured and escaped again, but fortunately he was recaptured immediately after. That man deserved to be hanged; he was what we knew as a "killer", and if he had been hanged, he certainly would not have murdered the other man. That would have had a deterrent effect, I am sure.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen will say
that if the young man had been kept in prison, the second murder would not have occurred. It is quite a common occurrence

in the West for men to escape from prison, but I never knew a man to escape after he had been hanged. In the early days of British Columbia, before we had so many theorists abroad in the land, we had a judge named Begbie, a man pretty well known throughout America. He was a man of magnificent physique, wonderful mental qualities and absolutely fearless. In those days we had bad men coming into British Columbia from Arizona, ' California anc Mexico. Judge Begbie would go north by himself, and if he could not find a man tc hang a murderer whom he had found guilty, I believe he would have hanged him himself. He may have done so on one occasion. He sentenced a number of people to be hanged, and the name of Judge Begbie was known through the whole of the Northwest. When bad men would come to Victoria, or Vancouver, which was a hamlet in those days, people would say to them:	"Watch
cut or Begbie will get you". His name was known throughout the whole Pacific coast. I cannot say whether Judge Begbie considered that the hangings were a deterrent for murder, but every man in British Columbia would agree with me in saying that they had a deterrent effect. We had law and order throughout British Columbia when we had a turbulent population there, and it was due to the fear of that judge that we had law and order at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I had not thought to discuss this question, but I have had some experience with condemned criminals. I was, for a part of my early life, one of the managers of a large penitentiary, and I came into contact with a number of men who were under the death penalty. I feel the responsibility that rests upon us as members of this parliament in casting our vote upon this question, our responsibility to the criminal and our responsibility to the men, women and children of Canada. We are told that sometimes innocent men are found guilty. That is very rare in these days, it is so rare that no such thing can be found, or, at least, in no such case is capital punishment inflicted. We are told that some mentally deficient people commit murder. True, but they are not subject to the law which we are discussing.
The question for us to determine to-night is whether we shall permit any criminal, no matter how fully matured he may be, no matter how dastardly may be his crime, no matter how long he may have premeditated it, to offend against society with impunity in the total absence of the death penalty? I

Capital Punishment
am not prepared to advocate any such thing. It is said that capital punishment is not a deterrent. Well, let a man be convicted of murder and sentenced to execution and immediately he and all his friends bestir themselves to have that sentence commuted to life imprisonment- Why? The penitentiary looks like a paradise to that man. Is capital punishment a deterrent? Ask yourselves the question. Which would you rather take a chance on-the penitentiary or the gallows? That is the question. What criminal finds it difficult to secure an associate? It is the criminal who has the reputation of being a killer. His fellow associates steer clear of him because they know that, if he does kill, his crime will bring down the extreme penalty of the law upon himself and his accomplices. The death penalty is a deterrent because as soon as men are aware that it faces them they begin to do everything in their power to have the sentence commuted. Take the case of a man who with gun in hand enters your house, steals your property and shoots down any man, woman or child that happens to be in his path to thwart him. He has that, deliberate, well-formed purpose in his heart, and he goes from your house to another man's, and possibly another's and kills three or four, being finally arrested and convicted. Now, our Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) says he ought to have a chance to reform. I say, that kind of a man has put himself beyond any state of that kind. He is given an ample opportunity to square himself with his Maker if he wants to improve his time, but generally such men do not do this; they forfeit all claims upon humanity. Such a man is an outcast, an outlaw. Cain it is said was not hanged. Well, Cain did not know what the effect of hitting a man on the head -with a club would be because he was the first fellow that tried it; they could not convict a man of premeditated murder in those days when a man did not know anything about murder. But where a man deliberately and premeditatedly goes out to kill he puts himself beyond the pale of human sympathy, and we should exercise ourselves not in sympathy with the criminal but in sympathy with the thousands of men, women and children throughout the country whose lives are in our keeping-Human life is too cheap in Canada to-day. Look at such incidents as have occurred in Montreal. The thing for us to do at this time is to maintain the supreme punishment. It may not deter everybody, because what will deter one man will not deter, another, and vice versa; and I think that everything we can do to prevent crime we should do today.

I had not intended taking part in the debate, but within the last few minutes an argument in favour of the retention of the death penalty has struck me and I think perhaps hon. members may feel its force as I do. There is in this matter the element of protection to society. We are all aware of that natural instinct of the human heart to resent as strongly and as energetically as possible any injury which has been done to us or to those who are near and dear to us. We know the old biblical law, an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. Every one of us, I think, has that desire, in some degree, to avenge himself on those who have done him a wrong. This feeling, as we can see throughout the pages of history, has been inherent in man from time immemorial. In times before law and order was enforced, when the savage, barbaric instincts held full sway in the heart of man, it was the generally recognized thing, when the member of a family had been killed who himself was guiltless, for those who belonged to him to take the life of the slayer. That, as the Solicitor General (Mr. McMur-ray) observes, is the avenge of blood. Now, whatever we may say to the contrary, this feeling still animates mankind; and in order to obviate the taking of justice by private individuals into their own hands society has decreed that the law shall avenge crime and see to it that retribution shall overtake the criminal. The surest evidence that this feeling still prevails is to be found in what is happening in the United States. There, as has been pointed out, law enforcement has fallen into disrepute. It has been found that murderers are not punished, so that men are taking the law into their own hands and applying the principles of lynch law while the state has neither the power nor the energy to intervene to protect the rights of private citizens from violators of the law. Unless therefore some measures are taken, cruel though they may appear, barbaric as they may seem to some hon. gentlemen, but necessary for the protection of society, we shall have private citizens, without the sanction of the law, and without giving to the murderer a fair trial, executing vengeance upon those who take life.
My hon. friend from East Calgary stated, with that sincerity and conviction which we all admire, that the onus of proving that the death penalty should be maintained is on those who urge its retention. Let me call his attention to the fact that the verdict of history is in favour of those who wish to retain capital
Capital Punishment

punishment, and that throughout the ages it has been found to be the only means of deterring people from committing this crime. He is on safer ground when he argues that we cannot produce statistics, for not every man who feels like committing murder goes about telling his neighbours that he does not do so because he is afraid of the hangman's rope. If we could collect statistics of such people who were deterred by reason of their fear of the death penalty, I think the figures would prove overwhelmingly the contention of . those who are opposed to the bill.
The hon. member also debated with the Minister of Justice the propriety of his referring to certain statistics respecting the death penalty for desertion during the recent war. He stated that the cases were not similar, that in war men's minds were abnormal. In my view his argument only strengthens the position of the Minister of Justice. After all, the soldier who did not desert because he feared the death penalty had been taught-with all due respect to the hon. member who says we are as guilty as the hangman-to be a killer; that was his job. If he was a well-trained soldier he should have had no respect for human life, yet when he was told he would be shot if he was found deserting in face of the enemy he remained at the post of duty.
The hon. member also stated, with some degree of warmth, that the members of this and preceding parliaments were individually and collectively in the position of the common hangman. The answer it seems to me is very simple. It is true we are responsible for the death penalty, but as yet we have not asked anybody to commit the crime which is punishable by that penalty.
Neither has the hangman.

That is true, but the hangman comes in after, and he has not had an opportunity of warning the gentleman for whom he performs this final office that he will be hanged if he does a certain thing; whereas we have.
Harrowing stories were related by the Solicitor General which to my mind went to show the fallibility of our laws rather than their injustice and cruelty. If our institutions were such that no crime could be committed, then I think his argument would be perfectly sound. But he argues that an innocent man may suffer the death penalty. And the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) said he would be prepared to abolish capital punishment rather than see one innocent man hanged. I think the argument works both ways. If, as the hon. Minister of Justice says,

the death penalty prevents one single murder, then it has justified its existence. It is true that to take away the life of an innocent, man is regrettable, but, after all, as has been well said, he has had ample time to arrange matters with his Maker, he has been surrounded with all the consolations which religion can afford him, he has had all the sympathy which sickly sentimentalists may give him. and in many cases he has had every opportunity of having his case fully placed before the public and even of going to his death in a fashion which, to his mind, deserves glorification. Under the circumstances I cannot help but feel that in the present state of our civilization, until such time as we all become so perfect that there will be no possibility of anyone committing murder, and there is no longer in the heart and mind of the human race any fear of death, we must retain the death penalty.

It seems
to me, Mr. Speaker, that law is the mother of liberty, but liberty so guarded that it guarantees the freedom of all. Are we to preserve that liberty in Canada by allowing criminals at large or by dealing lightly with them? I do not think that it is in the best interests of this country that we should do so. A good deal has been said by the supporters of this bill in sympathy with the criminal, but very little sympathy has been extended to their victims. A few evenings ago I read in the paper that a man hired another to kill his wife, and while she was engaged in prayer the assassin took her life, the callous husband standing by. Are men of that type entitled to any consideration? Is the supreme penalty not good enough for them? I do not think anything is too severe for such people.
Now, one hon. member here mentioned the returned soldier, and suggested that as the men had been accustomed when at the front to take life, that had an influence on their conduct in this country. I take that insinuation as an insult to our returned men. It is not the returned soldier who is committing murder, it is rather the slacker who remained at home who is doing it. I do not think that any insinuation of that kind should be made in this House against our returned men.

Mr. Speaker, I would not like to let this occasion pass without stating my position in the matter.
I have listened to the discussion with a great deal of interest, and we must all admit that there is a great deal of argument on both sides. It is very easy to present a very strong

Capital Punishment
case when only one side of it is dealt with.
I do not wish to go into the matter at length, because it has been dealt with in all its phases by others who have taken part in the debate. But there is no doubt that the responsibility in this matter is upon parliament. As the leader of this group (Mr. Forke) says, the responsibility is not with the jury, it is not with the judge, it is with parliament that makes the laws for Canada. I am willing to take that responsibility, but I must vote what I consider to be the right way in the matter.
We must deal with people as they are, not as we would like them to be, and we must take the necessary action to-day, not at some time in the future. If we pass this bill abolishing capital punishment, we
11 p.m. must take the responsibility. I do not say that hon. gentlemen arguing in favour of the bill are not perfectly willing to assume that responsibility, but I want to tell the House that I am not ready to assume it, because I am not convinced that it is a safe proposition. It would seem to me that more sympathy has been evidenced in this discussion for the criminal than has been evidenced for the public. We owe protection to the public, and I am afraid that there would not be as much protection if we abolished capital punishment, and that is my reason for voting against this bill. I want to feel while I live in Canada that I have the very best protection that human effort can give me. I do not say that any law can control all the factors in the situation. I believe that murders have been committed when no thought was taken by the offender as to whether he would be hanged or would go to the penitentiary. Where premeditated murder is committed I contend that it is not fair to show greater sympathy to the offender than is shown to the public. If I thought that imprisonment for life would be as effective as the death penalty in the case of murder I certainly would feel like supporting this bill, but I do not believe that life imprisonment is a sufficient deterrent. I do not believe that the public would get the same protection from the life imprisonment sentence that they would get from the continuance and enforcement of the capital punishment system.
Of course, in common with every other hon. member of the House, I must follw my. judgment in a matter of this kind. I have had my mind made up on the subject for a good many years. There was a time when I rather felt I would like to see capital punishment abolished) That was a good many years ago, and just about that time one of the states in the Union abolished capital punishment. I watched the effects of that
change, and I became convinced from the results shown that capital punishment was a greater deterrent, because more murders were committed in that state when capital punishment was abolished. Subsequently the death penalty was restored in that state, and crime then decreased. I do not know about many of the other . states, but that was the result in one case which I myself observed. Since then I have watched the matter very closely.

Will my hon. friend say
what state he refers to, what were the years in question, and what were the figures?

I do not know just the
years; I have no record of it except in my memory. I am not certain whether it was Massachusetts or Connecticut, but it was one of those two. But I do not think it matters what the particular state was or just what the year was; the matter was impressed on my mind at the time and now I am convinced that the same result will follow in any case where capital punishment is abolished. I would like to feel that it would be safe to abolish capital punishment, and I have always felt like giving any criminal a fair chance. But the public must be protected, and to that end I must lay aside my personal feelings and do what I believe is best for the people generally.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to take part in this debate, but on account of the turn it has taken I feel that I should put myself on record and state the reason for the attitude .1 intend to take when the question comes to a vote. The hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) has suggested that those supporting this bill seem to be more anxious to protect the murderer than to protect society. From my close attention to the debate, I have not understood the support to this bill, in that way. I feel that the supporters of this bill are just as anxious to safeguard society as any who have expressed an intention of voting against it. The hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride) said that he was not in favour of criminals going at liberty. I do not think any of us are, but the trouble is that there are too many criminals at large all the time. The probability is that there are far more criminals at liberty than are ever caught, and they are not criminals of the type that usually are caught and who eventually get sent to the gallows.
In my opinion there are many murders brought about indirectly. You find crime
Capital Punishment

wherever there is great poverty. You find more crime in the larger cities than you do in the country because there is greater poverty there. Wherever there is a large amount of wealth taken from the masses of the people and poverty created thereby, there you are most liable to have crime; but the real murderers in many cases are perpetrators of the schemes by which the people are taxed to the extent of their wealth.
The hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) made mention of the fact that a large percentage of the crimes committed in this country were committed by foreigners. I submit Mr. Speaker, that those foreigners did not come from the northern part of Europe, but probably from the great centres of Europe where the standard of living was very low indeed, and it was because of that standard of living and because of their environment, that after they came to .this country a certain percentage of them have been added to our list of criminals. An instance came to my mind the other day of a death that was caused at a large meeting of the depositors of the Home Bank. A woman overcome with despair at the loss of all she had in the failure of that bank died at that meeting. 'Who will say that the murderer of that woman could not be found among the officials that have been guilty of wrong doing in regard to the Home Bank? I think there has not been sufficient stress laid in regard to those criminals, who are either never caught, or are in such a position that there is very little chance of their ever going to the gallows. Wherever you find poverty, and especially great poverty, you will find crime, and when you do away with poverty you will do away with crime. For that reason I am willing to support the bill before the House because I believe that the great thing for us to do is to pay more attention to our social laws, and try to improve society, so that in the future there will be less and less crime and such laws as we have in the criminal code to-day making it possible to take away life will be unnecessary.

I must at the outset, Sir, state that
I am in favour of maintaining capital punishment, and therefore I shall vote against the proposed amendment of the hon. member for East Oalgary (Mr. Irvine). Our laws governing the death penalty are similar to those in force in England, France and the United States. We are therefore keeping good company. These laws have borne the test of time, and I think

we should preserve them such as they are. If I understand rightly the spirit of the law, our legislation as regards the death penalty, makes a distinction between two classes of murderers. There is, first, the man who is a danger to society, the criminal who is no longer in a position to appreciate human life. Such a person is really a social danger, and, it behoves society to do away with him. It is the duty of those in authority to exercise a guardianship, to protect the life of innocent persons by suppressing this degraded man, this human brute. Our legislators like those of other civilized countries have justly maintained the death penalty.
Besides this degraded murderer there exists another class of assassins which is met with in these distressing days when one of our fellow-creatures' life is treacherously cut short. I am referring to the person in whom murder is an event really accidental. Indeed, among those who have committed homicide, we have often noticed that the murderer was a good and respectable person, well thought of by his fellow-citizens. One day, under the influence of anger and passion he strikes one of his fellow-men. In the life of this man murder is purely an accident. We are at a loss to account for it. The public looks upon such a sad event as a regrettable accident. This murderer is not like the one previously mentioned, a degraded citizen, one who may be termed a brigand, a wild beast. He is rather a citizen of high moral standing, who, on the spur of the moment, committed homicide; he is the victim of passing passion which, for the time being, has deprived him of his senses and judgment. I think there should exist some clemency for this man. Our Canadian legislators have made provision for the case of an accidental murder in the life of a good citizen. Indeed, article 1077 of the Criminal Code states that an appeal can be made to the Governor-in-Council and that the death sentence pronounced against such a murderer may be commuted to a life sentence.
I am, therefore, of the opinion owing to all these reasons, that our laws are equitable, because they aim at punishing as it deserves the degraded murderer, and that on the other hand they give, protection to the person who, in a moment of aberration, has caused the death of one of his fellow-citizens. I am, therefore in favour of maintaining our laws and I shall vote against the proposed amendment.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. W. CALDWELL (Victoria and Carleton):
speechtext:
At this hour I will not detain the House at any great length. However, on account of the fact that I have repeatedly

Capital Punishment
expressed myself as opposed to the imposing of the death penalty, and on account of the fact that I propose to vote against the passing of the bill, I desire to make a brief explanation. As I said before I have repeatedly expressed the opinion that I was not in sympathy with the imposing of the death penalty. However, Mr. Speaker, considering the fact that there is at the present time a wave of crime sweeping over the country, I think it is a very inopportune time to abolish the death penalty. In the case of those who have so actively engaged in crime, and those who are possibly contemplating the carrying on of crime, it would be like handing them a reprieve in. advance. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I feel that I should make this statement before I vote against the bill.

It has been a pleasure to me to listen to this debate. I hope that all hon. members who have spoken on this subject, on whatever side they may have argued, will have said what they may wish they had said twenty years from now; and if they have, then I am not afraid of their happiness in the future. Much has been said about feeling, and if I have any criticism to make of those who have opposed the measure, it will be largely because they have been feeling a great deal more than they have been reasoning. Although I have detected, I think, a slight inclination on the part of one or two hon. members in their minds to creep out after their feelings in a search for any real basis upon which to justify themselves in supporting capital punishment as we now have it. I crave the indulgence of the House for a few minutes in order to go over some of the matters that have been advanced as arguments. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Caldwell) has given us a very strong argument for the abolition of capital punishment. He tells us that under capital punishment crime has been increasing , so rapidly that he would be afraid to try anything else. That is a strong argument.
I rise to a question of privilege. I did not make any such statement. I do not wish the hon. member to put words in my mouth.

I did not say he made
sudh a statement. I was simply giving his argument. We have capital punishment now, have we not? The hon. member has always been in favour of abolishing it, he says, but crime is so bad under capital punishment that he is afraid to abolish it. Is that not his argument? I do not think I am misrepresenting him at all. Then the hon. mem-84
ber for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) tells us that he is convinced that if capital punishment were abolished crime would increase, because at one time he was in a state-in Kentucky or Massachusetts, one of those two he is not quite sure-and while he was in that state a great wave of crime swept over the state, and he concluded that it was on account of the abolition of capital punishment. Now,' unfortunately for the hon. gentleman neither of those two states which he was convinced he was in has abolished capital punishment yet. The states which have abolished capital punishment are, Arizona, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Minnesota, North Dakota, South Dakota, Rhode Island, Tennessee-

I would like to refute
what the hon. gentleman has been saying, but he talks so "easy" I hardly think it is worth while.

If I thought the hon. member could refute me I would not talk so "easy," in fact I would talk harder if I thought he would find time to refute my statements. I have given him facts. I cannot help it if they have not abolished capital punishment in these states mentioned by him, but- these are the actual facts.

If the hon. gentleman
talked a little louder I could hear him. I could not .hear him, and I could not keep very good track of all he said.

The next hon. gentleman
who attempted to argue against the measure proposed was the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Power). I am sorry to see he is not in his seat, but his objection was that if we abolished capital punishment the same thing would happen in Canada as happened in the States, which, according to his argument, was that lynching became very popular. Now my hon. friend said in his opening remarks that he just got that idea while in his seat. I think that if he had got the idea two weeks ago and verified his idea with facts, he would not have made the speech that he made. I must quote facts again with regard to the point he raised. I will quote from a volume which is at the disposal of hon. members of this House in the Parliamentary Library. The quotation is as follows:
But we are told that if the state will not execute the people will; that lynchings which have discredited us in the eyes of the civilized world, are the direct result of our failure to apply the death penalty with promptitude and celerity. Even so distinguished a publicist as Dr. Andrew D. White, if the newspapers quote him aright, is inclined to this opinion, and under certain conditions

Capital Punishment

is disposed to regard lynching with favour as an abridgment of the law's delay. If this opinion be correct, as numerous writers aver, we shall of course, find the majority of lynchings in the states that have abolished the death penalty. What are the facts? In the last fifteen years two of these states have had not a single lynching. Of the others one has had two lynchings and the other four, while Georgia, the state that leads all others, with 172 executions, also stands second, with 237 lynchings. Texas follows with 140 executions and 183 lynchings. Alabama almost duplicates the record, with 119 executions ancj 206 lynchings; while Mississippi, which falls a little behind with 97 executions, leads all the states with 249 lynchings. Of 1,900 executions and 2,240 lynchings in the United States in the last fifteen years, twelve states, with less than one-third of the total population, performed, 1.090 executions and 1,747. of the lynchings. Almost without exception executions and lynchings go hand in hand. This fact that "he who runs may read" should dispose forever of the excuse that the state must execute to prevent the people from taking the law into their own hands.
My hon. friend ran so fast that he evidently did not read at all.

What is
the title of the book that the hon. gentleman is reading from?
It is the Debaters' Handbook on Capital Punishment.
Written many years ago.

My hon. friend also advanced another argument before he took his seat. I think we must give him the credit of putting capital punishment on its proper basis, namely, revenge. He found, that there is revenge in all human life; that out of revenge, capital punishment had developed, and by revenge, capital punishment had been sustained. We must give him cedit for being absolutely honest in his utterance; but he said that if we can prove one single case of murder that capital punishment has prevented, that would justify the continuation of capital punishment. I agree with him; but does my hon. friend mean to say that a single case has been proven by any hon. member of this House to-day? Not at all. In fact, I do not recall any hon. member having made an attempt to prove that. Those who have expressed their opinions in opposition to this measure have said with great firmness that they believe capital punishment is a deterrent; that they have a feeling it would restrain criminals; that they are afraid to alter the present law lest crime would increase, or some such statement; but no one has made an attempt to prove the deterring influence of the death penalty.
The next hon. member that I want to comment briefly upon is the hon. member for Battleford (Mr. McConica). He thinks capital punishment is a deterrent, He has no proof

except himself. He says-I am paraphrasing his argument now; I am not quoting it- hon. members of this Housce should ask themselves: What stops you from committing murder? Is it not the gallows you see rising up in your imagination? What am I to infer from the argument of my hon. friend? Am I to suppose that the only reason why he does not make an attempt on the life of the Prime Minister is that after he has figured out all the ways in which he might do that, the gallows come right in front of him, cowardly fear turns him aside and he refuses to commit the murder? Is that the argument that he has put forward?
I suggest that the victim that he looks for is more likely to be the hon. member for East Calgary (Mr. Irvine).

In that case I am profoundly glad that there is something that stays the hand of the hon. member for Battleford.
I come to the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael), who had never heard that Moses was a barbarian, and who had discovered that the New Testament taught something much more noble as a standard of living than that of the Old Testament. But he shakes hands, good-bye, to the New Testament, and he says that we must go back to Moses, back to the "eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth," back to the law of the jungle.
