We must despair of anything like Christianity becoming a practicability in this world. But what that has to do with the abolition of capital punishment, I am afraid I did not catch.
I come to the argument of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). If I recall aright, he opened his argument by putting himself and the Right Hon. Arthur Henderson in the same position, and he said that the Right Hon. Arthur Henderson was considering this matter very carefully. I hope that when the Right Hon. Arthur Henderson has concluded his consideration and given the result of his deliberations to the world, he will give us more reasons for maintaining capital punishment than the Minister of Justice has done. I say that, will all respect to the undoubted ability of the Minister of Justice. I think the House will agree with me; if they do not now, I would ask them again to read his arguments to-morrow, and I think they will agree with me that he did not give us a real argument, He spoke of a high sense of duty, which no doubt he has. He gave us his convictions. I believe he was sincere, and as such, I respect his sincerity and I hope he will mine. But that is not an argument. I cannot accept the sincerity, or conviction, or

Capital Punishment
mere belief of the Minister of Justice. I have assumed that we are living in a reasoning age, and also that this parliament is a place of reason, although the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) says that he made up his mind a number of years ago, so that all the arguments to-day have been wasted as regards himself. I have, however, assumed that this is a place where we listen to reason, and I look for reasons. I tried to base my arguments on reason; I carefully avoided making an appeal to passion. I or any other hon. member could stand up in this House and make an appeal on the basis of emotion that would make you cry for the sake of the prisoner. You could also make a man cry in thinking of the victim, as the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) attempted to make us do. So I avoided studiously making this argument on the basis of emotion and mere superstitious belief; I placed it on the basis of reason, brought up the facts of science as put forward by modern criminologists and penologists, and I have challenged the Minister of Justice or anyone else to give us a single instance, a single proof in favour of the argument that capital punishment deters crime, but instead of argument we are given belief. No mere belief is sufficient. This is far too important a question for us to settle upon a mere single belief of any man, I do not care how sincerely he holds that belief. So I looked to the Minister of Justice in the hope that he would be able to convince me if I were wrong, because I want to change if I am wrong. I hoped that he would show me the errors in my reasoning if there were any but he did not do so. He said that he did not wish us to think that revenge was the basis; but revenge is the basis whether we think it is or not. There is the fact. Then he insists that capital punishment is a deterrent; but the amount of energy that a man puts into his fist when he insists that it is a deterrent, does not make it a deterrent. The sound of his voice does not make it a deterrent. Even an emphatic rap on the desk does not make it a deterrent. Only facts make a deterrent, and those facts have not been given to the House.	.
Even the hon. member for West' Toronto (Mr. Hocken) follows the line of reasoning of the Minister of Justice, and he wishes us to accept his ipse dixit without any further argument. He is assured that capital punishment deters. That assurance is not enough.
I come to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen). It was left for him to' make the boldest attempt of all and he told us that if he had the slightest notion that we were in S4i
danger of losing the protection of the gallows, he would have come to this argument with more fire, witli more enthusiasm and better -I do not know whether I should say, informed-at least with better arguments; but inasmuch as he felt that the gallows were perfectly safe and that this method of meting out punishment would last for a long time yet, he did not put forth his largest guns. Then he proceeded to examine the law, and he pointed out to us that the law was very narrow in its application to murder. I am not a lawyer, of course; but I should like to read to the House just how loose, or narrow rather, this application is. I am reading from sections 259 and 260 of the Criminal Code at page 77:
Culpable homicide is murder,-
(a)	if the offender means to cause the death of the person killed;
(b)	if the offender means to cause to the person killed any bodily injury which is known to the offender to be likely to cause death, and is reckless whether death ensues or not;
(c)	if the offender means to cause death, or being so reckless as aforesaid, means to cause such bodily injury as aforesaid to one person, and by accident or mistake kills another person, though he does not mean to hurt the person killed;
(d)	if the offender, for any unlawful object, does an act which he knows or ought to have known to be likely to cause death, and thereby kills any person, though he may have desired that his object should be effected without hurting any one. 55-56 V., c. 29, s. 227.
260. In case of treason and the other offences against the King's authority and person mentioned in Part II, piracy and offences deemed to be piracy, escape or rescue from prison or lawful custody, resisting lawful apprehension, murder, rape, forcible abduction, robbery, burglary or arson, culpable homicide is also murder, whether the offender means or not, death to ensue, or knows or not that death is likely to ensue,-
It would appear therefore that there is nothing narrow about the application in so far as the criminal code is concerned. The leader of the opposition was rather careful to emphasize the coldJblooded murders. But had he known a little more about the subject he would have realized that the cold-blooded murder, although it is perhaps the more culpable in the eyes of the law, is really the less culpable from the scientific standpoint; for only a man who is lacking in some fundamental human trait could actually sit down and in cold blood calculate the means whereby to take the life of a fellow man. And that is one of the outstanding arguments in favour of the abolition of capital punishment. The man who is so lacking either in mentality or in morality as to figure a murder cold-blooded is * the kind of man who should not be punished by the kind of death which he has visited upon some one else. He is the man that ought to be protected against himself while we protect society from him.

Capital Punishment
The leader of the opposition does not consider that there is much in my argument in regard to the causes of crime; he does not regard it as sufficient to say that crime is caused by hereditary influences aggravated by the influences of environment- But he accepts the hypothesis for the sake of argument. Well, he should have followed it to its logical conclusion. Had he done so he would have realized that thex-e should be no place for punishment, on that assumption. And yet he speaks of punishment. But in this respect he misrepresented what I said. I said that there was no place for punishment, but I did not mean that thei'e was no place for prisons. I rather insisted that our attitude with respect to the prisoner should not be influenced by any considei-ation of punishment; but that does not mean that the criminal should roam ai'ound the country committing crime. The member for Kindersley (Mr. Carmichael) was of the opinion that some prisons were quite attractive, so attractive indeed that he would almost like to go there himself. He rather indicated that they were better 'than home. Well, that is the sort of prison that I should like to see established. That however is not to be interpreted as a suggestion that we should put a px'emium upon crime. The fact is that we recognize the importance of treating criminals in the way we treat our insane and diseased people. Concluding his speech the right hon. gentleman emphasized the necessity of protecting society, - failing to realize that capital punishment does not serve this end. Let me point out the difference between capital punishment and life imprisonment from the standpoint of the actual protection which is afforded human life- To-morrow moi'ning some man commits a murder. Well now, the offence has been perpetrated, and whatever steps may be taken to protect society thereafter, society certainly had not been protected before. The leader of the opposition would put this man upon the gallows and let him hang on a rope; I on .the other hand would put him in gaol or confine him in an insane asylum, according to the diagnosis of a competent person. I would not take his life. But in each case he would be pi-evented from killing any one else. My system would equally protect society, because my right hon. friend's method undoubtedly did not protect the life of the man that was killed. As an hon. gentleman observed, the man could not kill anybody else after he had been hanged, nor under my system would he be able to commit the crime again. So that there is no argument left my right hon. friend. The leader of the opposition made a pathetic appeal to senti-

ment. Let me assure him that there is something wrong with legislators who have to fall back upon the gallows as a protection to society, and I hope that he will discover where the weakness is.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), accepting the arguments of the leader of the opposition, deplores the onerous task that devolves upon him under the present law; and on being asked to give a reason for the- perpetuation of the thing that gives him such an unpleasant duty he replies that statistics can prove anything, and on this ground refuses to give any. Unfortunately there is a great deal of truth in that. But surely the Prime Minister would not like hon. members on this side of the House to test the merits of his budget by that principle. Figures can prove anything, certainly; and no doubt it can prove a surplus where a deficit actually exists. The Pi-ime Minister, I say, would not like to have his budget analyzed in that fashion. We must stop somewhere with that kind of criticism, and while I know that figures may be misleading, at the same time the leader of the government might have favoured the House with one citation, let us twist it as we might, to prove our justification in maintaining capital punishment. I agree that his task is a difficult one under the present law. He tells us that he feels the solemnity of the matter; I hope we all feel it. But the Prime Minister might feel more solemn if next week he sanctioned the regular course of the law, and the execution therdby of an innocent man. In order to save him some of that awful anxiety and to free him from the solemn responsibility of that onerous duty I would urge him to vote for this measure and at least give it a trial. Let us try it for one year, and we can keep our eye on the hon. member for Battleford (Mr. McConica) for that length of time. Then, if we have not all killed one another in the interval, we might extend the period of trial to two years. That is the only way we can prove the efficacy of such a new law; and I have so much faith in humanity, and in Canadians particularly, that I do not believe that the number of murders would be increased in any degree whatever by the enactment of this bill.
